a: The LORD called to Moses
p: The book's Hebrew name is its first word, Vayiqra, "and he called." It picks up where Exodus stopped.
b: Jewish tradition names Leviticus Vayiqra, "and he called," from its first word. "Leviticus" comes from the Greek and Latin title, "the book about the Levites," though it is really about the priests, Aaron's family, and the whole people. Exodus ends with the glory filling the tent, so that "Moses could not go into the tent of meeting" (Exodus 40:35). Leviticus opens with God calling him from inside it. In Hebrew scrolls the last letter of vayiqra, an aleph, is written small. Rashi says the full word is a call of love, while God met Balaam with a bare vayiqar, "he happened upon" (Numbers 23:4). "The LORD" stands for God's personal name, YHWH, as in most English Bibles.

a: presents an offering
p: Korban, "offering," comes from the verb "bring near." Mark 7:11 quotes the word.
b: The general word for an offering, qorban, comes from qarav, "come near, bring near." Chapters 1–7 use the verb again and again: the worshiper "brings near" (the Plain English says "presents") his offering, and the priest "brings near" the blood. An offering is a way of approaching God. Jesus quotes the word in Aramaic form in Mark 7:11, where something declared "Korban," which means a gift, could no longer help one's parents. Josephus also explains korban as "gift" (Against Apion 1.167).

a: When any one of you
p: The word is adam, "a human." The rabbis allowed non-Jews to send burnt offerings to the Temple.
b: The law begins with adam, "a human being," not "an Israelite." Rashi links it to Adam: as the first man owned everything and stole nothing, so an offering must be one's own. The rabbis also ruled that non-Jews could vow and send burnt offerings to the Temple, though not the other kinds (Talmud, Menachot 73b, deriving it from the "any man" of 22:18). History bears this out: Josephus says a daily sacrifice was offered in Jerusalem on behalf of the Roman emperor, and that stopping it in AD 66 was the act that began the war with Rome (Jewish War 2.409). Solomon had prayed that foreigners too would pray at the temple (1 Kings 8:41–43).

a: present your offering from the livestock
p: Was sacrifice a concession to an ancient habit, or a picture of the worshiper giving himself? Two famous answers.
b: Moses Maimonides (about 1190) argued that God allowed sacrifice because Israel, coming out of a world where every nation worshiped this way, could not have accepted a religion without it. God redirected the custom to himself and limited it to one place and one family, preparing for prayer (Guide 3.32, 46). Ramban (about 1270), commenting on 1:9, rejected this sharply: Noah and Abel offered before any idolatry, and the text calls sacrifice "a soothing smell." For him the worshiper should see in the animal what he himself deserves, its blood for his blood, its body burned for his body, and offer it as a substitute by God's mercy. Both readings still have defenders in Judaism and Christianity. See also the chapter page.

a: burnt offering
p: Olah means "what goes up." Except for the hide (7:8), the whole animal rose to God in smoke.
b: The olah is named from the verb "go up": all of it goes up in smoke. The Greek translation called it holokautōma, "wholly burned," the source of the English word "holocaust." It is the oldest and most common offering in the Bible. Noah offers it after the flood (Genesis 8:20), Abraham is told to offer Isaac as one (Genesis 22:2), and Job offers burnt offerings in case his children have sinned (Job 1:5). Leviticus lists it first, and says it was "to make atonement" for the one who brings it (1:4), even though no sin is named. Many read it as an act of total surrender to God. The worshiper gets nothing back to eat.

a: a flawless male
p: Tamim means whole, complete, sound. The same word describes Noah and is asked of Abraham.
b: Tamim means whole or without anything missing. Leviticus 22:17–25 lists what disqualifies an animal: blindness, broken bones, sores, damaged parts. The prophet Malachi accuses priests of offering blind and lame animals they would not dare give the governor (Malachi 1:8). The same word is used of people: Noah was "blameless" (tamim) in his generations (Genesis 6:9), and God told Abraham, "Go about your life in my sight, and be whole" (Genesis 17:1). The New Testament applies the picture to Jesus, who "offered himself unblemished to God" (Hebrews 9:14), like "a lamb with no flaw or spot" (1 Peter 1:19).

a: He is to lean his hand on the head of the burnt offering
p: Is the hand a sign of ownership, of identifying with the animal, or of passing sin to it?
b: The verb samakh means to lean or press with weight. The rabbis said the worshiper pressed "with all his strength" (Talmud, Chagigah 16b). What it meant is debated. (1) Ownership: "this animal is mine, offered for me" (Milgrom, David P. Wright), since a gift must be clearly given by someone. (2) Identification: the worshiper puts himself in the animal's place, so that its death stands for his (Ramban, Wenham, many Christian readers). (3) Transfer of sin: as Aaron puts Israel's sins on the goat with both hands (16:21). But that goat is not sacrificed, and Wright argued that two hands mark transfer while one hand marks ownership. The same gesture later gave its name to rabbinic ordination, semikhah (Numbers 27:23).

a: to make atonement for him
t: Kipper: cover, wipe clean, or ransom?
p: The key verb of Leviticus. Scholars argue whether it means to cover, to purge, or to pay a ransom.
b: Kipper appears almost fifty times in Leviticus 1–16. Its root is debated. (1) "Cover," from an Arabic word, an older view ("covering" sin from God's sight). (2) "Wipe off, purge," from Akkadian kuppuru, used of rubbing a temple clean in Babylonian rites (Milgrom, Levine). This fits the atonement "for" an altar or a house (8:15; 14:53), which cannot sin. (3) "Ransom," from the noun kofer, a payment that buys a life (Exodus 30:12; 21:30), which fits 17:11, where blood is given "for your lives." Jay Sklar argues that in Leviticus kipper often means both: a ransom that also purifies. The English "atonement," made standard by William Tyndale, means "at-one-ment," making two parties one.

a: He is to slaughter the young bull
p: The worshiper himself slaughtered the animal. Only the blood work belonged to the priests.
b: The verb shachat means to slaughter by cutting the throat. Here "he," the worshiper, does it, and the priests take over at the blood. The Mishnah agrees that slaughter by a non-priest was valid (Zevachim 3:1). In Ezekiel's vision Levites do the slaughtering for the people (Ezekiel 44:11), and in Chronicles the Levites help when there are too few priests (2 Chronicles 29:34). The method, a quick cut across the throat, was later regulated in Jewish law as shechitah and is still used for kosher meat. The ordinary Israelite was not a spectator. He brought, leaned, killed and cut up his own animal.

a: splash it all around the altar
p: Zaraq means to throw or dash a quantity of blood, not to sprinkle drops. That is a different verb.
b: Two verbs for blood rites run through these chapters. Zaraq (here) means to throw liquid from a bowl, so the blood was dashed against the altar. The rabbis said it was thrown at two opposite corners so that it reached all four sides (Mishnah Zevachim 5:4). Hizzah (4:6; 16:14) means to spatter drops with the finger. The KJV and the word list give "sprinkle" for both, which hides the difference; the Plain English has "splash" and "spatter." Why blood on the altar? Leviticus gives its reason later: "a body's life is in its blood," and God has given it "on the altar, to make atonement for your lives" (see 17:11).

a: a soothing smell for the LORD
p: The phrase first appears when God smells Noah's offering and promises never again to curse the ground.
b: Reach nichoach is literally "a smell of rest" or "of calming." It first appears after the flood: "The LORD smelled the soothing smell, and the LORD said in his heart, 'I will not curse the ground any more because of humankind'" (Genesis 8:21). The offering quiets anger and pleases God. The prophets warn that the smell means nothing when life is wrong: "I will not smell your soothing smells" (26:31; Amos 5:21). Paul uses the Greek form for Christ, who "handed himself over for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God, a sweet smell" (Ephesians 5:2), and for gifts from the churches (Philippians 4:18).

a: an offering by fire
t: Offering by fire, or food gift?
p: Ishsheh looks like 'esh, "fire," but some scholars think it means "gift" or "food offering."
b: The traditional rendering (KJV "an offering made by fire") links ishsheh to esh, "fire." But the word is also used of things not burned, such as the bread of the Presence and its frankincense (24:7–9), and the wine poured out. Milgrom and others connect it with an Ugaritic word meaning "gift," and some modern versions give "food offering." Since the meaning is unsettled, the Plain English keeps the familiar sense, which fits most uses, and notes the other here. Either way the phrase marks something given over to God at the altar.

a: turtledoves or young doves
p: A bird earns the same words as a bull: "a soothing smell." The Mishnah drew a famous lesson.
b: Turtledoves and young pigeons cost little, and Leviticus repeatedly allows them for those who cannot afford a sheep (5:7; 12:8; 14:22). The bird offering ends with exactly the same words as the bull: "a burnt offering, an offering by fire, a soothing smell for the LORD" (1:17; 1:9). The Mishnah draws the lesson at the end of the tractate on grain offerings: "Of the burnt offering of cattle it is said 'a soothing smell,' and of the burnt offering of birds 'a soothing smell' ... to teach that it is all one, whether a person offers much or little, so long as he directs his heart to heaven" (Menachot 13:11). Jesus' parents would bring the poor offering (12:8; Luke 2:24).

a: its crop with its feathers
p: The Hebrew can mean "with its feathers" or "with its filth." Interpreters split.
b: Notsah is rare. The Greek and the KJV take it as "feathers," and that is its sense in its other uses (Ezekiel 17:3, 7; Job 39:13). Rashi, following the rabbis, takes it as the bird's "filth," the waste in the gut, and so many modern versions say "contents." The word list follows the first view, and the Plain English keeps it, but either way the point is the same: parts that are not food are thrown on the ash heap east of the altar, not burned on it. The ash heap was on the side facing the entrance, away from the holy place.

a: a grain offering
p: Minchah means "gift" or "tribute." Cain's gift in Genesis 4 is a minchah.
b: Outside Leviticus minchah is a gift that honors a superior: Jacob's present to Esau (Genesis 32:13), the tribute Ehud carried to the king of Moab (Judges 3:15). Cain's and Abel's offerings are both called minchah: "Cain brought some of the fruit of the ground as a gift to the LORD" (Genesis 4:3). In Leviticus the word is narrowed to an offering of flour, oil and incense. Every Israelite household made bread, so this was the offering anyone could bring. The prophets look forward to a day when "in every place" a pure minchah will be offered to God's name among the nations (Malachi 1:11).

a: When anyone presents
p: Here the word for "anyone" is nefesh, "soul." The rabbis saw the poor man offering himself.
b: Chapter 1 began with adam; this law begins with nefesh, "a soul, a person." The rabbis asked why. "Who usually brings a grain offering? A poor man. The Holy One says: I count it as if he offered his very soul" (Talmud, Menachot 104b; Rashi on 2:1). A handful of flour from someone who has little is, in God's eyes, a whole life given. The story of the widow's two small coins (Mark 12:41–44) makes the same point.

a: frankincense
p: A costly resin from trees of southern Arabia and Somalia, carried north on camel caravans.
b: Levonah, "the white stuff," is the dried sap of Boswellia trees, which grow in southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa. It was carried north along the incense road, and Jeremiah speaks of it coming "from Sheba" (Jeremiah 6:20). It was expensive, so it was put on the grain offering but burned whole with the token portion, not eaten. It was also part of the holy incense (Exodus 30:34) and was laid on the bread of the Presence (24:7). The wise men's gift to the child Jesus included it (Matthew 2:11).

a: token portion
p: Azkarah, from "remember." The Greek word for it returns in Acts 10:4, for Cornelius' prayers.
b: Azkarah comes from zakhar, "remember." Only a handful is burned; the rest goes to the priests (2:3). Many think the portion "reminds" God of the worshiper, or stands for the whole as a token. The Greek translation renders it mnēmosynon, "memorial." Luke uses the same word when the angel tells the Roman officer Cornelius, "Your prayers have gone up before God, and your alms too, as a remembrance" (Acts 10:4), as if his prayers were a grain offering rising from the altar. The incense of prayer is a similar picture (Psalm 141:2).

a: It is a most holy part
p: Leviticus ranks offerings: "most holy" ones are eaten only by priests in the sanctuary court.
b: The Hebrew is "a holy thing of holy things." Leviticus sorts the offerings into two grades. "Most holy" offerings (grain, sin and guilt offerings) may be eaten only by male priests, inside the sanctuary court (6:16, 26; 7:6). "Holy" offerings, such as the priests' share of the peace offering, may be eaten by priests' families in any clean place (10:14). The same phrase names the inner room, "the most holy place" (Exodus 26:33). Philip Jenson calls this a "graded holiness": the closer to God, the stricter the rules.

a: any yeast or any honey
p: Both cause fermenting. Some saw a picture of corruption; Maimonides saw a rejection of pagan worship.
b: "Honey" here likely includes date or fruit syrup, the usual sweetener; bees' honey was rarer. Both yeast and honey were allowed as gifts to the priests (2:12; 7:13; 23:17) but never burned on the altar. Explanations: (1) Both cause fermentation and decay, which does not belong at the altar of the living God (Philo, many modern scholars). The New Testament uses yeast as a picture of spreading corruption (1 Corinthians 5:6–8; Matthew 16:6), though Jesus also uses it for the kingdom (Matthew 13:33). (2) Maimonides said idolaters offered leavened bread and sweet things, so Israel was to avoid them (Guide 3.46). Hittite and Mesopotamian texts do mention honey offered to gods, so his guess has some support.

a: the salt of your God's covenant
p: Salt does not rot. A covenant "of salt" was one that lasts, sealed perhaps by eating together.
b: Salt preserves and does not spoil, so a "covenant of salt" means a lasting one: God's gifts to the priests (Numbers 18:19) and the kingship of David's line (2 Chronicles 13:5). Eating salt with someone created a bond. Persian officials wrote, "we eat the palace's salt" (Ezra 4:14), meaning they were in the king's service. Ezekiel's temple offerings are salted too (Ezekiel 43:24), and the Mishnah describes a salt chamber in the temple. Jesus said, "Everyone will be salted with fire" and "Keep salt in yourselves, and keep peace with one another" (Mark 9:49–50), sayings many link to this verse.
r: Numbers 18:19; 2 Chronicles 13:5; Ezra 4:14; Ezekiel 43:24; Mark 9:49–50; Matthew 5:13

a: young ears of grain roasted in the fire
p: The word aviv, "young ears," also names the spring month when barley ripened and Israel left Egypt.
b: Aviv is barley in the ear, still green, and gave its name to the spring month of the exodus (Exodus 13:4). Karmel is fresh grain, roasted and crushed into a coarse meal. The rabbis tied this verse to the barley sheaf (omer) brought on the second day of Passover (see 23:10–14), and so read it as barley rather than wheat. Roasted grain was everyday food: Boaz gave Ruth some (Ruth 2:14).
orig: אָבִיב קָלוּי בָּאֵשׁ גֶּרֶשׂ כַּרְמֶל (aviv qalui ba'esh geres karmel)

a: a sacrifice of peace offering
p: From the root of shalom. Most of the animal was eaten by the worshiper's family in a feast.
b: The zevach shelamim is the one offering ordinary Israelites ate. The fat went to God, the breast and right thigh to the priests (7:30–34), and the rest to the family and guests, eaten the same day or the next (7:15–16). Its name is from the root of shalom. Translations try "peace," "fellowship" and "well-being." Rashi gave the rabbis' explanation: it is called shelamim "because it brings peace into the world," and because there is a share for the altar, the priests and the owners. Unlike the burnt offering, a female animal was allowed. Meat was rare in daily life, so this was a feast.

a: the fat that covers the insides
p: Chelev is the hard fat around the organs, not the fat marbled in the meat.
b: Chelev is the suet that covers the stomach, kidneys and liver. The rabbis distinguished it from shuman, the fat in the muscle, which may be eaten, and Jewish law still removes the chelev (and the sciatic nerve, Genesis 32:32) from kosher meat. The fat was treated as the best part, which is why "fat of the land" means its richest produce (Genesis 45:18). Abel brought "of their fat" (Genesis 4:4). Eli's sons took meat before the fat was burned, and the text calls it a great sin (1 Samuel 2:15–17).

a: the whole fat tail
p: Near Eastern sheep store fat in a heavy tail. Herodotus describes tails so big they rode on little carts.
b: The common sheep of the Near East, like the Awassi breed today, has a broad tail of fat that can weigh many pounds. The Greek historian Herodotus said some Arabian sheep had tails so long that shepherds built small carts to carry them (Histories 3.113). The tail was counted among the fat and burned on the altar. In 1 Samuel 9:24 Samuel gives Saul the thigh "and what was on it," which some think was the fat tail, as an honor portion.

a: It is food
p: Neighboring religions fed their gods twice a day. Israel kept the word "food" but rejected the idea.
b: The fat is called lechem, "bread, food," and elsewhere the offerings are "the food of their God" (21:6; Numbers 28:2). In Mesopotamia and Egypt the gods' statues were served real meals each day, and the Babylonian flood story says the gods, starving after the flood, "gathered like flies" around the sacrifice. Israel kept the old word but not the belief. There is no statue to feed and no meal set before it. A psalm has God say, "Suppose I were hungry: I would not say so to you, for the world and everything in it is mine. Do I feed on the flesh of strong bulls? Do I drink goats' blood?" (Psalm 50:12–13). Verdict: a real shared vocabulary, deliberately reinterpreted.

a: before the LORD
t: God's name in a Greek scroll
p: A Greek Leviticus scroll from Qumran writes God's name as IAO here, not "Lord."
b: Most Greek Bibles we have, all copied by Christians, put kyrios, "Lord," for YHWH. But a papyrus scroll of Leviticus 2–5 in Greek from Qumran Cave 4 (4QpapLXXLev-b, first century BC) writes the name as ΙΑΩ, Iaō, at 3:12 and 4:27. Patrick Skehan, who published it, argued that early Jewish Greek copies wrote out the divine name in some form, and that "Lord" came in later. Others think different Jewish communities simply did different things. Either way it is one of the oldest witnesses to how the name was handled in Greek.

a: you must not eat any fat or any blood
p: The ban on blood goes back to Noah. The early church kept it for Gentile believers (Acts 15).
b: The blood rule is older than Sinai. God told Noah, "flesh with its life, its blood, you must not eat" (Genesis 9:4). Leviticus repeats it (7:26–27) and gives its reason in 17:10–14: the life is in the blood, and God has given blood for atonement. Fat is banned only from sacrificial animals (7:25). When the apostles in Jerusalem decided what Gentile Christians must keep, they asked them to abstain from "blood" and "what is strangled" (Acts 15:20, 29), echoing Genesis 9 and Leviticus 17. The rule has shaped kosher practice ever since, and some Christian groups still keep it.
r: 7:23–27; 17:10–14; Genesis 9:4; Deuteronomy 12:16; Deuteronomy 12:23–25; Acts 15:20; Acts 15:29; 1 Samuel 14:32–34

a: sin by mistake
p: Shegagah: a wrong done without meaning to, or without knowing it was wrong. Defiant sin is different.
b: The sin offering of chapter 4 covers shegagah, a wrong done by accident or in ignorance. The opposite is sin "with a high hand," in open defiance, for which Numbers 15:30–31 says no offering is given. Milgrom argued that the category was wide, covering negligence as well as true accidents, and that 5:20–26 (6:1–7 in English) shows even deliberate wrongs could be brought once the person repented. The Psalms pray for both: "Who notices his own slips? Clear me of faults I cannot see. Hold your servant back from arrogant sins too" (Psalm 19:12–13). Hebrews 9:7 says the high priest offered blood for the "errors" (agnoēmata) of the people.

a: the anointed priest
p: Mashiach, "anointed," here means the high priest. It is the word that becomes "messiah."
b: Only the high priest had the oil poured on his head (8:12), so he is "the anointed priest" (also 6:22; 16:32). The word mashiach later names Israel's kings, "the LORD's anointed" (1 Samuel 24:6), and in time the coming king, the Messiah. In Greek it is christos. The Dead Sea Scrolls expect two anointed ones, "the messiahs of Aaron and Israel," a priest and a king (Community Rule 9:11). Hebrews brings the two together in Jesus, a king who is also high priest.

a: as a sin offering
p: Hatta't means "sin" and also "de-sinning." Milgrom said it purifies the sanctuary, not the sinner.
b: Hatta't is spelled like the word for "sin," but it comes from a form of the verb that means to clear of sin or purify, the verb used when Moses "cleansed the altar from sin" (8:15). It is required where no sin is involved: after childbirth (12:6), after a discharge (15:15), at the end of a Nazirite vow (Numbers 6:14), and for a new altar. So Jacob Milgrom called it the "purification offering": its blood is a kind of "ritual detergent" that cleans the sanctuary of the pollution caused by sin and impurity, while the sinner's remorse takes care of the sinner. Others (N. Kiuchi, Roy Gane, Jay Sklar) accept the purifying role but argue that the offerer, too, is cleansed and forgiven (4:26). Sklar calls the effect "ransom-purgation": one rite both pays for the sinner's life and cleanses the stain. The Plain English keeps the traditional name and notes the debate.

a: brings guilt on the people
t: A leader's sin falls on everyone
p: When the high priest sins, the whole people share the guilt. Rank decides the size of the offering.
b: Chapter 4 moves down a ladder: anointed priest, whole community, leader, ordinary person. The higher the rank, the larger the animal and the deeper into the sanctuary the blood goes. For the priest and the community, blood is brought inside to the incense altar and the veil (4:5–7, 16–18), as if their sin had polluted the tent itself. For a leader or a commoner, the blood touches only the outer altar. The high priest represents the nation, so his error is the nation's. The prophets often blame priests for leading the people astray (Hosea 4:6–9; Malachi 2:7–8).

a: seven times
p: Seven, the number of completion, governs the blood rites, the days of ordination and the cleansings.
b: Blood is spattered seven times here and on the Day of Atonement (16:14, 19), oil seven times on the altar (8:11), and blood or oil seven times for the healed person and the house (14:7, 16, 51). Ordination lasts seven days (8:33), and most impurities end after seven days. Seven recalls the seven days of creation and the Sabbath, and marks a thing as fully done. Naaman washed seven times in the Jordan and his skin was healed (2 Kings 5:14).

a: outside the camp to a clean place
t: Burned outside, but in a clean place
p: What is left of the priest's sin offering is not garbage. It is burned in a clean place.
b: The bull of the sin offering for the priest or the people is not eaten, because the priest cannot profit from his own atonement (6:30). Its remains are burned outside the camp. Yet the place must be "clean," the spot where the altar ashes are taken (6:11). Holy remains must not be dumped among the unclean. The Hebrews passage on Jesus suffering "outside the gate" (Hebrews 13:11–13) is discussed in the note on Exodus 29:14.

a: and become guilty
p: Asham may mean "be guilty" or, as Milgrom argued, "feel guilty," the inner sting that leads to the offering.
b: The verb asham recurs through 4:13–5:26. Most translations render it "incur guilt" or "be guilty." But Milgrom noticed that it often comes where the sin is still hidden (4:13; 5:17), and argued for "feel guilt": the person realizes something is wrong, even before he knows what, and so brings the offering. Others reply that the verb describes a real state before God, whatever one feels. The difference matters for 5:17, which says a person who sins without knowing it "has become guilty."

a: and they will be forgiven
p: The passive verb leaves the forgiver unnamed: it is God's act. The priest makes atonement; God forgives.
b: The pattern is always the same: "the priest will make atonement ... and he will be forgiven." The verb salach, "forgive," is used in the Bible only with God as subject. The priest does the rite, but forgiveness is not automatic. The prophets attack offerings brought without changed lives (Isaiah 1:11–17; Amos 5:21–24), and Leviticus itself requires confession (5:5) and repayment (6:4–5). The Mishnah sums it up: "The sin offering and the guilt offering atone; death and the Day of Atonement atone, together with repentance" (Yoma 8:8).

a: A leader may sin
p: The rabbis read the opening word, asher, as ashrei: "happy" is a generation whose leader owns his error.
b: The laws for the priest and the people open with "if" (im), but the leader's law opens with asher, "when." Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai heard in it ashrei, "happy": "Happy is the generation whose ruler brings a sin offering for his mistake" (Talmud, Horayot 10b; also Rashi). The leader, nasi, was a tribal chief (Numbers 7:2). Later the word became the title of the head of the rabbinic court. The point: the text assumes leaders will sin, and expects them to admit it.

a: It is a sin offering.
p: The Greek Bible's name for this offering, "for sin," appears in Romans 8:3, and maybe in 2 Corinthians 5:21.
b: The Greek translation usually calls the hatta't "(the offering) for sin," peri hamartias, or simply "sin." Paul writes that God sent his Son "in the likeness of flesh that sin rules, and as a sin offering" (Romans 8:3). The Greek behind "as a sin offering" is peri hamartias, which many translators take that way. In 2 Corinthians 5:21, "God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us," some interpreters, from Augustine on, read "sin" as "sin offering," as in this Greek usage; others think Paul means that Christ took on the state of sin. Hebrews 10:6 and 10:8 quote Psalm 40 using the same phrase.

a: the common people of the land
p: Am ha'arets here means an ordinary Israelite. In rabbinic times it came to mean an uneducated person.
b: In Leviticus the phrase means any Israelite who is not a priest or leader. Elsewhere it can mean the landholding citizens who acted together in politics (2 Kings 11:14–20; 21:24). After the exile it named the non-Jewish population of the land (Ezra 4:4). In the rabbinic period an am ha'arets was someone careless about tithes and purity, or simply uneducated, and the Pharisees kept a distance from them (John 7:49 shows a similar attitude). Here there is no contempt: the commoner has his own offering, a female goat or lamb, smaller than a leader's.

a: he hears the public curse calling for witnesses
t: A public curse on hidden witnesses
p: When a crime was unsolved, a curse was proclaimed on anyone who knew and kept silent.
b: The alah is a public oath or curse: "cursed is whoever saw and does not testify." Micah's mother pronounced one over her stolen silver, which made her son confess (Judges 17:1–2). Proverbs warns that the thief's partner "hears the curse spoken and says nothing" (Proverbs 29:24). At Jesus' trial the high priest put him under such an oath: "I put you on oath before the living God: tell us" (Matthew 26:63), and Jesus answered. The silent witness "carries his guilt" and needs the offering of 5:6.

a: he is unclean
t: Unclean is not the same as sinful
p: Tame, "unclean," is a ritual state that bars a person from holy things. It is usually not a sin.
b: Uncleanness (tum'ah) comes from death, from the body's flows and from certain animals. It is caught by touch, it lasts a set time, and it is removed by waiting, washing and sometimes an offering. It is not wrong to be unclean: people had to bury the dead and have children. What is wrong is to bring uncleanness near holy things, or to neglect cleansing, as here, where a person forgets he touched a carcass. Jonathan Klawans calls this "ritual impurity" and separates it from "moral impurity," caused by grave sins like murder and sexual crimes, which pollutes the land itself (18:24–28). See 11:24 and chapter 15.

a: speaking rashly with his lips
p: A careless oath still binds. Ecclesiastes and Jesus both warn against easy swearing.
b: The verb means to blurt out without thinking. An oath to do harm or good, once spoken, is binding, and forgetting it is a fault. The Bible's warning stories include Jephthah's vow (Judges 11:30–39) and Saul's oath that nearly killed Jonathan (1 Samuel 14:24–45). Ecclesiastes advises, "Do not rush to open your mouth ... Not vowing is better than vowing and not paying" (Ecclesiastes 5:2–5). Jesus goes further: "Do not swear at all ... Let your word be 'Yes, yes' or 'No, no'" (Matthew 5:33–37; James 5:12).
r: Numbers 30:6–8; Judges 11:30–39; 1 Samuel 14:24–45; Psalm 106:33; Ecclesiastes 5:2–5; Matthew 5:33–37; James 5:12

a: he is to confess the sin he has committed
p: The first time the law demands spoken confession. It became central to Jewish and Christian repentance.
b: Hitvaddah means to declare openly, to own up. Here and in Numbers 5:7 the law requires words, not just an animal. On the Day of Atonement the high priest confesses the people's sins aloud (16:21). Maimonides opens his Laws of Repentance by deriving from Numbers 5:7 that every commandment's breach requires spoken confession before God. The Jewish prayers Ashamnu ("we have been guilty") and Al Chet ("for the sin") are said on Yom Kippur. Christians read 1 John 1:9: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive." Psalm 32:5 describes the relief.

a: his guilt payment
p: Here asham means the penalty paid for guilt, even though the animal is a sin offering.
b: This verse uses asham, but what is brought is "a sin offering." So asham here is not the name of a kind of offering (that comes in 5:14) but the "penalty" or "payment" owed. The KJV's "trespass offering" and many modern versions' "guilt offering" can blur this. Milgrom called the offering of 5:14–6:7 the "reparation offering" for the same reason: it repays. Chapter 5:1–13 is often called the "graded" sin offering, because the cost goes down to fit the person's means.

a: If he cannot afford a sheep
p: The law scales the cost to the purse: sheep, then birds, then a little flour.
b: The Hebrew says "if his hand does not reach," an idiom for "if he cannot afford," as the Plain English has it. The law steps down from a lamb or goat, to two birds, to a tenth of an ephah of flour (about two quarts or two liters). No one is shut out from atonement because he is poor. The same ladder appears after childbirth (12:8) and for the healed person (14:21–22). The New Testament records Mary and Joseph bringing "a pair of turtledoves or two young doves" (Luke 2:24), the poor family's offering.

a: a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a sin offering
p: A sin offering of flour, with no blood at all. Hebrews 9:22 says "almost" everything is cleansed with blood.
b: For the poorest, a handful of flour serves as a sin offering. It has no oil or frankincense, so that it is not mistaken for a gift of joy. This is the clearest case in the law of atonement without blood. Hebrews seems aware of it: "by the law almost everything is made clean with blood, and without blood poured out there is no forgiveness" (Hebrews 9:22). The rabbis noted that flour atoned only where the law allowed it, and that blood remained the rule (see 17:11).

a: act unfaithfully
p: Ma'al means breaking faith, especially by taking what belongs to God. Achan is the classic case.
b: Ma'al is a betrayal of trust, used of a wife's unfaithfulness (Numbers 5:12) and of Israel's unfaithfulness to God. In priestly law it means "sacrilege": misusing something holy, such as eating a priest's portion or keeping a tithe. Achan took devoted plunder from Jericho, and the text calls it ma'al (Joshua 7:1). King Uzziah broke faith by burning incense himself and was struck with skin disease (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Milgrom showed that the guilt offering is required for exactly this: sacrilege against holy things, and false oaths that misuse God's name (6:2–3).

a: as his guilt offering
t: Isaiah's servant as a guilt offering
p: Isaiah 53:10 says the servant's life is made an asham. Christians and Jews read the servant differently.
b: The asham is a payment that makes up for harm done to God's holy things or to his name. Isaiah's song of the suffering servant uses the word: "if his life is made a guilt offering (asham), he will see offspring" (Isaiah 53:10). Christian readers from the New Testament on (Acts 8:32–35; 1 Peter 2:22–25) see Jesus, whose death repays a debt he did not owe. Jewish interpreters such as Rashi and Ibn Ezra read the servant as the people of Israel, suffering among the nations, or as a prophet. Either way Isaiah borrows the language of this chapter: a life given to make good what others took.

a: add a fifth to it
p: The wrongdoer repays what he took and adds a fifth. Only then does the offering atone.
b: The order matters: first restitution, then the ram. A fifth, or twenty percent, is added as a penalty, both for holy things (here) and for wrongs against a neighbor (6:5; Numbers 5:7). Theft discovered by others cost far more: double, or four or five times for animals (Exodus 22:1–4). The lower rate here rewards the person who comes forward on his own. Zacchaeus, the tax collector, offers more than the law asked: "if I have squeezed anything out of anyone by false charges, I pay it back four times over" (Luke 19:8).

a: without knowing it
p: From this verse the rabbis made an offering for cases where a person was not sure he had sinned.
b: This law covers someone who has done wrong without knowing it, or who suspects but cannot be sure. The rabbis built on it the asham talui, the "suspended" guilt offering, brought when a person did not know whether he had sinned: for example, he ate one of two pieces of fat, one forbidden and one allowed, and could not tell which (Mishnah Keritot 4:1). The Mishnah tells of one pious man, Bava ben Buta, who brought one every day just in case (Keritot 6:3). The verse takes seriously that people can be guilty and not know it, a point Psalm 19:12 also makes.

a: The LORD spoke to Moses.
p: In Hebrew Bibles 6:1–7 is 5:20–26, and 6:8–30 is 6:1–23. This site uses the English numbers.
b: The chapter break falls in a different place in Hebrew and English Bibles. Hebrew Bibles (and Jewish translations such as the JPS) end chapter 5 with these seven verses, so English 6:1–7 is Hebrew 5:20–26, and English 6:8 is Hebrew 6:1. The English numbering goes back to the Latin Vulgate's chapter divisions, which were added in the 1200s. The weekly synagogue reading Tzav, "Command," begins at English 6:8. When reading a Jewish commentary on these verses, subtract or add the difference.

a: act unfaithfully against the LORD by cheating his neighbor
t: A wrong to a neighbor is a wrong to God
p: Cheating a neighbor is called "unfaithfulness against the LORD." The false oath made God a party to the lie.
b: Every case in 6:2–3 is a wrong against another person: denying a deposit, robbery, extortion, keeping lost property. Yet the text calls it ma'al, sacrilege "against the LORD." Milgrom's explanation is the false oath of 6:3: the wrongdoer swore by God's name that he had nothing, dragging God into his lie. Rabbi Akiva drew a wider lesson in the Sifra: one who denies a neighbor denies the God who witnessed their deal. David says the same after wronging Uriah: "You, you alone, are the one I sinned against" (Psalm 51:4). The law also shows a deliberate sin (lying under oath) being atoned once the person confesses and repays.

a: on the day he admits his guilt
p: Repayment to the victim comes before the offering to God. Jesus taught the same order.
b: The wrongdoer repays the owner in full plus a fifth (see 5:16), and only then brings his ram (6:6). "The day of his guilt" may mean the day he is found out, or, as Milgrom argued, the day he feels his guilt and comes forward. Jesus kept the same order: "Suppose, then, you are presenting your offering at the altar, and there it comes to mind that your brother holds something against you. Leave the offering where it is, before the altar, and go. Make peace with your brother first, and then come and present your offering" (Matthew 5:23–24). The Mishnah says the same of the Day of Atonement (see 16:30).

a: This is the procedure for the burnt offering
p: Torah here means a ritual procedure. Chapters 6–7 repeat the offerings as a manual for the priests.
b: Chapters 1–5 told ordinary Israelites what to bring. Chapters 6–7 go back over the same offerings from the priests' side: what the priest does, wears and eats. Each section begins "This is the torah of ..." (6:9, 14, 25; 7:1, 11), and 7:37 sums them up. Torah, often rendered "law," means instruction or teaching; here it is the set procedure. The order also changes: the burnt offering, which burns all night, comes first because it is always on the altar.

a: Then he is to take off these garments and put on others
p: The first job of the day was removing ashes in linen. In the temple, priests raced up the ramp for it.
b: Removing the ashes was the first act of each day, done in the holy linen clothes, though the priest changed to carry them out of the camp. In the Second Temple it became a coveted task. The Mishnah says priests once raced up the altar ramp to win it, until one pushed another off and broke his leg, after which the jobs were assigned by lot (Yoma 2:1–2; Tamid 1:2). The care taken with the ashes shows that even the leftovers of holy things were handled as holy.

a: Fire is to keep burning on the altar without a break
t: The fire that never goes out
p: The altar fire began with fire from God (9:24) and was to be fed by the priests forever.
b: The command is repeated three times in 6:9–13. The fire was lit by God himself (9:24), and from then on the priests had to keep it alive. Second Maccabees tells a legend that priests hid the altar fire in a well at the exile and found it again as a thick liquid when the temple was rebuilt (2 Maccabees 1:19–22). Fire temples in ancient Persia also kept sacred flames burning, a likely parallel in practice, though the meaning differs. Christians have used the verse as a picture of steady devotion: Paul calls believers to be "burning in spirit" (Romans 12:11).

a: Whatever touches them will become holy.
p: Most holy things passed on holiness by touch. The prophet Haggai tested the limits of the rule.
b: On the two possible readings ("becomes holy" or "must be holy") see the note on Exodus 29:37. Leviticus applies the rule to the most holy offerings (6:18, 27). Ezekiel says priests must change their clothes before going out to the people, "so that their clothes do not pass holiness to the people" (Ezekiel 44:19; 46:20), which assumes holiness could spread to people. Haggai asks the priests whether holy meat carried in a fold of a garment makes bread holy if the garment touches it; they say no, but uncleanness does spread (Haggai 2:11–13). Uncleanness was more catching than holiness.
orig: כֹּל אֲשֶׁר־יִגַּע בָּהֶם יִקְדָּשׁ (kol asher-yigga bahem yiqdash)

a: on the day he is anointed
t: On the day of anointing, or every day?
p: The offering is "continual," yet tied to "the day he is anointed." The rabbis split the difference.
b: The verse says both "on the day he is anointed" and "continually, half in the morning and half in the evening." The rabbis concluded that every ordinary priest brought this griddle offering once, on his first day of service, while the high priest brought it every day of his life (Mishnah Menachot 4:5; Rashi). Josephus also describes the high priest's daily offering of flour (Antiquities 3.257). Because the priest gives it, none of it may be eaten (6:23): a priest cannot eat his own offering.

a: The clay pot it is boiled in is to be broken
p: Porous clay soaks up what is cooked in it; bronze can be scoured. This is the root of kosher pot rules.
b: Unglazed clay absorbs what is cooked in it, so a clay pot that has held most holy meat cannot go back to ordinary use, and must be broken. A bronze pot can be scoured and rinsed. The same idea governs uncleanness: a clay pot that a dead swarming creature falls into is smashed (11:33; 15:12). Together with Numbers 31:22–23, these verses became the basis of the Jewish laws for making utensils kosher (kashering) by boiling or fire, and for keeping separate dishes.

a: if any of a sin offering's blood is brought into the tent of meeting
p: Hebrews uses this rule to say Christians eat from a sacrifice that priests of the tent could not.
b: When the sin offering's blood went inside the tent (4:5–7; 16:14–15), its meat was not eaten by anyone. Hebrews 13:10–12 builds on this: "We have an altar from which those serving in the tent have no right to eat." Jesus' death is like the Day of Atonement offering, whose blood entered the holy place. Some interpreters, especially Catholic and Orthodox, read the "altar" as the Lord's Supper, where believers share what was forbidden under the old rule. Others read it as the cross itself, or as the spiritual benefit of Christ's death, with no reference to the meal (Attridge, Koester survey the views).

a: the hide of that burnt offering belongs to him
p: Priests lived on shares of the offerings. A Phoenician price list shows the same system next door.
b: Priests had no land (Numbers 18:20), so their income came from the altar: hides of burnt offerings, most of the grain offerings, the meat of sin and guilt offerings, and the breast and thigh of peace offerings. The "Marseilles Tariff," a Phoenician inscription of about the 300s BC found in southern France, lists for each kind of animal what part went to the priests and what fee they were paid, including the hide. Eli's sons abused the system (1 Samuel 2:12–17). Paul cites it to defend paying ministers: "those who attend the altar take a share of the altar" (1 Corinthians 9:13).

a: If he presents it to give thanks
t: The thank offering will never end
p: A peace offering of thanks for rescue. The rabbis said it alone will remain in the age to come.
b: Todah means both "thanks" and "confession," giving credit where it is due. It was brought after a rescue: a recovery from illness, a safe journey, release from prison. Psalm 107 lists such rescues, and for those saved it says, "Let them sacrifice thank offerings" (Psalm 107:22). Psalm 100 is titled "a psalm for the todah." The rabbis taught: "In the time to come all sacrifices will cease, except the thank offering" (Leviticus Rabbah 9:7). Hebrews echoes the Greek name for it: "through him let us offer God a sacrifice of praise at all times, the fruit of lips that confess his name" (Hebrews 13:15).
r: 22:29; Psalm 50:14; Psalm 100:1; Psalm 107:22; Psalm 116:17; Jeremiah 33:11; Hebrews 13:15

a: bread made with yeast
p: Yeast was banned from the altar (2:11), but leavened loaves come with the thank offering for the feast.
b: Only a token loaf of each kind went to the priest (7:14); the rest, including ordinary leavened bread, was eaten at the family's feast. Since none of the leavened bread was burned, 2:11 is kept. A thank-offering meal had meat and four kinds of bread. The rabbis counted ten loaves of each kind, forty in all (Mishnah Menachot 7:1), enough to feed a crowd.

a: is to be eaten on the day it is offered
p: A whole animal eaten in a day meant inviting others. Proverbs shows such a feast at home.
b: A thank offering had to be eaten on the day it was offered; a vow or freewill offering could last into the second day (7:16). With no refrigeration, a family could not eat a whole sheep in a day, so they had to share with neighbors, the poor and the Levites (Deuteronomy 12:18–19). Milgrom thought the time limit pushed toward generosity and also kept holy meat from spoiling. Proverbs shows the darker side: the seductress says, "Peace offerings were on me; today I have paid my vows," so there is meat at home for a guest (Proverbs 7:14).

a: for a vow or is a freewill offering
p: Two more kinds of peace offering: one to keep a promise, one simply out of love.
b: A neder is a vow: "If you rescue me, I will offer." Jacob (Genesis 28:20–22), Hannah (1 Samuel 1:11) and Jonah ("I will pay what I vowed," Jonah 2:9) all made one. A nedavah is an offering no one asked for, given freely, the same word used for the gifts that built the tabernacle (Exodus 35:29). Psalm 66:13–15 describes paying vows with burnt and peace offerings. Paul paid the expenses of four men completing a vow in the temple (Acts 21:23–26).

a: It will be foul meat
p: Piggul, "foul, stale meat," became a rabbinic term for an offering ruined by wrong intention.
b: Piggul appears only here, in 19:7, and in two prophets: Isaiah condemns those who eat "broth of foul meat" (Isaiah 65:4), and Ezekiel protests he has never eaten piggul (Ezekiel 4:14). It is probably meat gone off. The rabbis read the verse in a surprising way: since an offering cannot be undone on the third day after it was accepted, they took it to mean that a priest who intended, while offering, to eat it too late made it piggul from the start (Mishnah Zevachim 2:2–3). The idea that intention can ruin a holy act became central to rabbinic thought about worship.

a: It will not be credited to him.
p: The same verb, chashav, says Abraham's trust "was reckoned" to him as righteousness.
b: A sacrifice eaten too late "will not be credited" to the worshiper. The verb chashav means to reckon or credit. Gerhard von Rad argued that priests formally "reckoned" an offering as accepted or not, and that Genesis 15:6 borrows this language for faith: Abram "put his trust in the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness." Paul builds Romans 4 on that verse. Not all scholars accept von Rad's priestly setting, but the shared verb is real (see also Psalm 106:31).

a: that person is to be cut off from his people
p: The penalty for eating holy meat while unclean. Does it mean execution, exile, early death or loss in the afterlife?
b: Karet, "cutting off," is threatened for about twenty offenses in the Torah, including eating blood (7:27) and failing to fast on the Day of Atonement (23:29). Views: (1) Not a human court's sentence but God's own act, since 20:2–5 separates execution by the people from God's "cutting off." (2) The rabbis said it meant early death or dying childless (Mishnah Keritot 1:1 lists the offenses; Talmud, Moed Katan 28a). (3) Milgrom and Donald Wold argued it means one's family line dies out and one is cut off from one's ancestors after death, the opposite of being "gathered to one's people" (Genesis 25:8). (4) Later Jewish and Christian practice sometimes read it as excommunication. Genesis 17:14 uses it for an uncircumcised male.

a: The fat of an animal that died or was torn by wild animals
p: An animal that died on its own, or was killed by a beast. The word "treif," non-kosher, comes from terefah.
b: Nevelah is an animal that died without being slaughtered; terefah is one "torn" by a wild animal. Exodus 22:31 already said: "Do not eat flesh torn by beasts in the field; throw it to the dogs." The meat makes a person unclean (11:39–40; 17:15). The rabbis widened terefah to any animal with a fatal defect found after slaughter. The Yiddish word treif, for anything not kosher, comes from it. Here the fat is still useful, for lamps or leather, but may not be eaten.

a: a wave offering
p: Tenufah, traditionally "wave offering." Some scholars think it was a lifting up toward God.
b: On the meaning of tenufah, waving back and forth or lifting up to present, see the note on Exodus 29:24. Here the worshiper's "own hands" bring it. The rabbis pictured the priest's hands under the owner's, waving the breast and fat together, so that the giver himself takes part. The motion was later echoed in the waving of the palm branch on the Feast of Booths (23:40).

a: This is the procedure for the burnt offering
p: After the Temple fell, the rabbis taught that studying these laws counts as offering the sacrifices.
b: The summary repeats torah, "procedure, teaching." The rabbis read it as a promise: "'This is the torah of the burnt offering': whoever studies the torah of the burnt offering is as if he offered a burnt offering" (Talmud, Menachot 110a, Resh Lakish). When the Temple was destroyed in AD 70, this teaching, along with prayer in place of sacrifice (Hosea 14:2, "let us pay you the bulls of our lips"), let Judaism keep Leviticus at the center. That is one reason Jewish children traditionally began their Bible study with Leviticus (Leviticus Rabbah 7:3).

a: The LORD commanded it to Moses on Mount Sinai
t: On Mount Sinai or from the tent?
p: 1:1 says God spoke from the tent; 7:38 says "on Mount Sinai." Two traditions, or one place?
b: The book opens with God speaking "from the tent of meeting" (1:1), but this closing line says "on Mount Sinai," and Leviticus ends the same way (26:46; 27:34). Traditional readers take "on Mount Sinai" loosely as "at Sinai," where the tent stood at the foot of the mountain; the Hebrew preposition can mean "at." Some rabbis held that the laws were given in general on the mountain and repeated in detail in the tent. Critical scholars see two layers, one that placed the giving of law on the mountain and another that placed it in the tent once built.

a: Take Aaron and his sons with him
p: Chapter 8 does what Exodus 29 commanded, step by step, with "just as the LORD commanded" seven times.
b: This chapter carries out the ordination rite God gave in Exodus 29, nearly word for word. The refrain "just as the LORD commanded Moses" comes seven times (8:4, 9, 13, 17, 21, 29, and in other words 8:36), the same refrain that ended the building of the tabernacle in Exodus 39–40. The obedience is stressed because the next story, chapter 10, is about disobedience. Small differences exist: the anointing of the tent and its furniture (8:10–11) comes from Exodus 30:26–29 and 40:9–11, not Exodus 29, and critics read the chapter as a later fulfillment report built from Exodus 29 and 40.

a: gather the whole community at the entrance of the tent of meeting
p: How could all Israel stand at one doorway? The rabbis called it a miracle; others read "community" as its leaders.
b: The courtyard entrance could not hold hundreds of thousands. Rashi, following Leviticus Rabbah 10:9, says: "This is one of the places where a small space held a great number." Many modern readers think edah, "community," here means the people's representatives, the elders, as it seems to in some other passages (compare 4:15). Either way the point is public: the priesthood was given before the whole people, not in secret.

a: He poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron's head
p: Only Aaron has oil poured on his head. Psalm 133 remembers the oil running down his beard.
b: On the oil poured on Aaron and the link to kings and to "messiah," see the notes on Exodus 29:7 and on 4:3. Here the order is striking: Moses first anoints the tent, its furniture and the altar (8:10–11), and only then Aaron. The priest is made holy as part of the holy place he will serve in. Aaron's sons are anointed later, by sprinkling with oil and blood (8:30).

a: and so cleansed the altar from sin
p: The verb is a form of "sin" that means to remove sin. David prays it in Psalm 51:7.
b: Vayechatte comes from the root chata, "sin," in a form that means to take sin away, to purify. It explains the name hatta't, the "sin offering" or "purification offering" (4:3). A new altar has done no wrong, yet it must be "un-sinned" and made holy before it can be used (Exodus 29:36). David uses the same verb of himself: "Take away my sin with hyssop, and I will be pure" (Psalm 51:7). See the note on 1:4 on kipper, which here, too, is done "on" an object.

a: on the lobe of Aaron's right ear, on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot
p: The same three points are marked on a healed outcast in 14:14. The priest and the leper share a rite.
b: On the usual reading (the whole person devoted to hearing, doing and walking) see the note on Exodus 29:20. Leviticus adds a surprise: the same marks, with blood and then oil, are put on a person healed of skin disease (14:14, 17). Milgrom suggested that the extremities, the points where the body ends, were protected or purified as a boundary. Mary Douglas read the two rites as matching passages from one state to another: the priest from common to holy, the healed person from outside the camp back to the community. In both, a person is brought across a line.

a: It was Moses' portion of the ram of ordination
p: For the seven days Moses does what priests do and gets the priest's share. He is never a priest again.
b: During the ordination Moses slaughters, handles the blood and burns the fat, and he receives the breast, the priest's portion. Psalm 99:6 remembers "Moses and Aaron among his priests." The rabbis asked what he wore and answered that he served "in a white garment without a hem" (Talmud, Avodah Zarah 34a). Moses, though, does not get the thigh, which will belong to the regular priests (7:32–33), and once Aaron is installed, Moses never offers again.

a: For it will take seven days to fill your hand.
p: The Hebrew idiom for ordination is "fill the hand." The Greek rendered it "make perfect," which Hebrews uses.
b: "To fill the hand" means to install someone in office. Micah "filled the hand" of a Levite to make him his priest (Judges 17:5, 12). Akkadian texts use a similar phrase for appointing officials, and some think the idiom first meant putting the first portions or the payment into the new priest's hands (as in 8:27). The ram of ordination is the "ram of filling" (millu'im). The Greek translation often renders the idiom "to make perfect" (teleioō). Hebrews plays on this: the law appointed weak men as high priests, "but the word of the oath ... sets up a Son, made perfect for all time" (Hebrews 7:28).
r: 7:37; 8:22; 16:32; 21:10; Exodus 28:41; Judges 17:5; Judges 17:12; Hebrews 2:10; Hebrews 5:9; Hebrews 7:28

a: Stay at the entrance of the tent of meeting day and night for seven days
p: Anthropologists call this a threshold time: the priests are no longer common but not yet at work.
b: For seven days Aaron and his sons may not leave the entrance. Anthropologists since Arnold van Gennep (1909) describe rites of passage in three steps: separation, a time "on the threshold" (the liminal stage, from Latin limen, "doorway"), and joining a new state. Leviticus fits remarkably well: washing and dressing (separation), seven days literally at the doorway (threshold), and the eighth day when they begin to serve (9:1). The same seven-plus-one pattern shapes the cleansing of the healed person (14:8–10) and the person with a discharge (15:13–14). Edmund Leach and Mary Douglas developed this reading.

a: On the eighth day
p: Seven days of creation, then an eighth: the day worship begins. Christians later called Sunday "the eighth day."
b: After the seven days of ordination comes the eighth day, when the priests begin and God's glory appears. Eight marks a new beginning: circumcision on the eighth day (12:3), cleansing completed on the eighth day (14:10; 15:14), the eighth day of the Feast of Booths (23:36). The rabbis dated this day to the first of Nisan, the first anniversary of the exodus month, and said "that day took ten crowns" (Talmud, Shabbat 87b): it was the first day of the week of creation, the first day of priestly service, the first day of offerings at one sanctuary, and more. Early Christians called Sunday, the day of the resurrection, "the eighth day" (Epistle of Barnabas 15:9; Justin, Dialogue 41).

a: a calf for a sin offering
p: Aaron's first offering is a calf. The rabbis heard an answer to the golden calf.
b: The word egel, "calf," is the word used for the golden calf Aaron made: "He took the gold from them ... and made it into a calf of cast metal" (Exodus 32:4). Nowhere else in Leviticus is a calf the sin offering. The Sifra and Rashi say this was to show that God had forgiven Aaron for the calf: the man who made the calf must now offer one. The Sifra adds that the people's male goat (9:3) answers the goat whose blood Joseph's brothers used to deceive their father (Genesis 37:31). Modern scholars generally see no hidden message, but the link with Exodus 32 is hard to miss.

a: so that the glory of the LORD may appear to you
p: All the ritual of chapters 1–9 aims at this: God showing himself to his people.
b: Moses promises that if the people do as commanded, "the glory of the LORD" will appear, and it does (9:23). The glory had filled the tent when it was built (Exodus 40:34), but now it shows itself to all the people at the altar. The sequence of offerings is significant: sin offering first (to cleanse), then burnt offering (to give), then peace offering (to share a meal). Many interpreters, Jewish and Christian, have seen in this order the path back to God: forgiveness, surrender, fellowship.

a: offer your sin offering and your burnt offering
p: The high priest must atone for himself before he can atone for others. Hebrews draws the contrast with Jesus.
b: Aaron offers first for himself (9:8–14), then for the people (9:15–21). Hebrews notes this: every high priest "is bound to offer for sins, for himself as for the people" (Hebrews 5:3), whereas Jesus "does not need, as those high priests do, to offer sacrifices day after day, first for his own sins and then for the people's" (Hebrews 7:27). The Greek text of this verse adds "and for your household," matching 16:6 (see the variant).

a: blessed them
t: The oldest Bible words ever found
p: The priestly blessing was engraved on two tiny silver scrolls found near Jerusalem, from about 600 BC.
b: Leviticus does not say what words Aaron used, but Numbers 6:22–27 gives the blessing priests were to speak: "May the LORD bless you and keep you. May the LORD make his face shine toward you ..." In 1979 Gabriel Barkay found at Ketef Hinnom, outside Jerusalem, two small rolled silver amulets with a version of these words. They are dated to about 600 BC and are the oldest known copies of any Bible text. Ben Sira describes the high priest Simon raising his hands to bless the people in the temple (Sirach 50:20–21), and Jesus blesses his disciples with lifted hands before he is taken up (Luke 24:50–51).

a: Fire came out from before the LORD and ate up the burnt offering
p: God answers with fire. The very same words begin the next disaster (10:2).
b: Several times the Bible shows God accepting an offering by fire: for Gideon (Judges 6:21), David (1 Chronicles 21:26), Solomon (2 Chronicles 7:1) and Elijah on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:38). Here the fire from God lights the altar that is never to go out (6:13). Then 10:2 repeats the words exactly: "Fire came out from before the LORD and ate them up." The fire that accepts can also destroy. The writer to the Hebrews draws the lesson: "our God is a consuming fire" (Hebrews 12:29, quoting Deuteronomy 4:24).

a: Nadab and Abihu
p: Aaron's two oldest sons. They had gone up Sinai and seen God and lived. Now they die at his altar.
b: Nadab and Abihu were the firstborn and second son of Aaron and Elisheba (Exodus 6:23). They had been among the few invited up the mountain: "They saw the God of Israel ... Against the nobles of the Israelites he did not put out his hand. They looked upon God, and they ate and drank" (Exodus 24:10–11). Now, on the first day of their service, fire from God kills them. They died without children (Numbers 3:4; 1 Chronicles 24:2), so the priesthood passed through Eleazar and Ithamar.
r: Exodus 6:23; Exodus 24:1; Exodus 24:9–11; Exodus 28:1; Numbers 3:2–4; Numbers 26:60–61; 1 Chronicles 24:1–2

a: strange fire, which he had not commanded them
p: The text says only that God had not commanded it. Readers have offered many reasons.
b: Esh zarah means "strange" or "unauthorized" fire (compare the "strange incense" of Exodus 30:9). Suggestions: (1) The coals were not taken from the altar, whose fire came from God (16:12; Numbers 16:46), the view of many modern scholars, including Milgrom. (2) They burned incense at the wrong time or in the wrong place, perhaps entering the inner room (16:1–2). (3) They were drunk, since the next law bans wine (10:9; Leviticus Rabbah 12:1). (4) Pride: they gave a ruling in front of their teacher Moses (Sifra; Talmud, Eruvin 63a), or wished Moses and Aaron dead to take over (Sanhedrin 52a). (5) Philo saw holy zeal that carried them into God's presence, a death that was a kind of rapture (On Dreams 2.67). The text gives no motive. Edward Greenstein argued that the silence is the point: the holy cannot be handled.

a: ate them up
p: Their tunics were not burned (10:5). The rabbis said their souls were burned, not their bodies.
b: The same fire that "ate up" the offering (9:24) now eats up the two priests. Yet their cousins carry them away "in their tunics" (10:5), so the clothes survived. The rabbis took this to mean the fire entered them, like "two threads of fire" through their nostrils, burning their souls but leaving bodies and garments whole (Talmud, Sanhedrin 52a). The plainer reading is that they were struck dead by God's fire, and the clothes are mentioned to show they were carried out as priests.

a: In those who come near me I will show myself holy;
p: No earlier verse says these words. Rashi pointed to Exodus 29:43, read in a new way.
b: Moses quotes God, but the saying is not found earlier in the Torah. Rashi found it in Exodus 29:43: "the place will be made holy by my glory (bikhvodi)," which he read as "by my honored ones." In his telling, Moses then comforts Aaron: "I knew the house would be made holy by those close to God, and I thought it would be you or me. Now I see they were greater than both of us." Modern readers take the saying as a short poem stating a principle: those closest to God are held to the highest standard. Amos says it to the nation: "You are the only ones I have known among all the clans of the earth ... That is why I will call you to account" (Amos 3:2).

a: And Aaron was silent.
p: Three words in Hebrew. The rabbis said God rewarded the silence by speaking to Aaron alone (10:8).
b: Vayyiddom Aharon: he did not protest, mourn aloud or defend himself. The verb is used of being stunned still (Exodus 15:16) and of silent trust (Psalm 37:7; Lamentations 3:28). The rabbis praised it: as a reward, the next speech (10:8) is addressed to Aaron alone, one of very few in the Torah (Rashi, following the midrash). Others hear grief beyond words. Job's friends sat with him seven days "Not one of them said anything to him" (Job 2:13). Some modern readers hear shock, even protest held in.

a: Do not let your hair hang loose or tear your clothes
t: No mourning in the holy place
p: Priests on duty could not show the usual signs of grief. At Jesus' trial the high priest tore his robes.
b: Loosening the hair (KJV "uncover your heads") and tearing clothes were ordinary mourning customs (13:45; Genesis 37:34). Priests anointed for service could not stop to mourn without making the holy place unclean, and the high priest could never do so (21:10). The whole people mourns instead. At Jesus' trial the high priest "tore his clothes" at what he took as blasphemy (Matthew 26:65; Mark 14:63), a gesture the rabbis allowed for blasphemy (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:5), though 21:10 forbade it to the high priest in mourning.

a: not to drink wine or beer
p: The only law God gives Aaron alone. Many read it as a hint about why his sons died.
b: Shekhar is any strong drink besides grape wine, mostly barley beer, the common drink of Egypt and Mesopotamia. Priests on duty must stay sober (also Ezekiel 44:21), so that they can make right judgments (10:10–11). Placed right after the deaths, the rule led some rabbis to conclude that Nadab and Abihu were drunk (Leviticus Rabbah 12:1). Proverbs warns rulers the same way (Proverbs 31:4–5), Isaiah mocks priest and prophet who "stagger from beer" (Isaiah 28:7), and Paul says, "Do not be drunk with wine ... Instead, be filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18).
r: Numbers 6:3; Ezekiel 44:21; Proverbs 31:4–5; Isaiah 28:7; Luke 1:15; Ephesians 5:18; 1 Timothy 3:3

a: You must separate the holy from the ordinary, and the unclean from the clean
p: Two pairs: holy or ordinary; clean or unclean. The rest of the book is built on them.
b: This verse is the key to Leviticus. Everything is either holy (belonging to God) or ordinary (chol, "common, everyday"). And everything is either clean or unclean. The ordinary can be clean or unclean; the holy must be clean. Milgrom drew it as a chart: the clean and ordinary can become holy through consecration, and the holy and the clean can be polluted by uncleanness; the danger is when the unclean meets the holy. Chapters 11–15 teach the clean and unclean; chapters 17–27 the holy. Ezekiel accuses the priests of his day of failing at exactly this (Ezekiel 22:26), and promises that they will do it again (Ezekiel 44:23).

a: You must teach the Israelites
p: Priests were not only for sacrifice. They were Israel's first teachers of God's law.
b: The priests' second task is to teach. Moses' blessing on Levi says, "They will teach your rulings to Jacob" (Deuteronomy 33:10). Malachi says, "A priest's lips are to keep knowledge, and people are to seek teaching from his mouth" (Malachi 2:7). Hosea blames the priests for the people's ruin: "My people are destroyed because they have no knowledge" (Hosea 4:6). After the exile Ezra, a priest, read the law to the people (Nehemiah 8). In time the rabbis, mostly not priests, took over this teaching role.
r: 14:57; Deuteronomy 17:9–11; Deuteronomy 33:10; Hosea 4:6; Haggai 2:11; Malachi 2:7; Nehemiah 8:1–8

a: searched hard
p: Scribes counted the Torah's words and letters. These two words were said to be its middle word.
b: The Hebrew darosh darash, "searching he searched," was counted by ancient scribes as the middle of the Torah by words. The Talmud reports that the early scribes were called soferim, "counters," because they counted every letter: the middle letter is the large vav in "belly" (11:42), the middle words are darosh darash (here), and the middle verse is "Then the person is to shave, but not shave the scaly patch" (13:33). The Talmud itself admits it was not sure (Kiddushin 30a). Modern counts of the standard text put the exact midpoints slightly elsewhere, but the tradition shows the care scribes took.

a: would the LORD have been pleased?
p: Aaron argues that grieving men should not eat holy food. Moses accepts the correction.
b: Moses expected the priests to eat the people's sin offering as 6:26 required. Aaron's answer is brief but pointed: after such a day, eating a most holy meal in mourning could not please God. Deuteronomy 26:14 shows that food eaten in mourning was unfit for holy use. Rashi and the Talmud (Zevachim 101a) say that Moses "was not ashamed to say, 'I did not hear,'" and admitted Aaron was right. A midrash (Leviticus Rabbah 13:1) adds that Moses sent a herald through the camp to say he had erred. The Torah keeps a story in which its great lawgiver is corrected.

a: these are the creatures you may eat
p: Hygiene, symbol, ethics, identity, or simply God's decree? Every major answer has its defenders.
b: The text gives only one reason: "be holy, for I am holy" (11:44–45). Readers have proposed: (1) Health: Maimonides held some such view (Guide 3.48), but many allowed animals are no safer, and the text never mentions health. (2) Order: Mary Douglas (Purity and Danger, 1966) argued that clean animals fit their realm's normal type and unclean ones are misfits; she later read the laws as protecting vulnerable creatures (1999). (3) Analogy: Gordon Wenham, building on Douglas, saw three ranks of animals (unclean, clean, fit for the altar) mirroring the nations, Israel and the priests. (4) Reverence for life: Jacob Milgrom argued that the system limits which creatures may be killed and, with the ban on blood, teaches respect for life. (5) Ethical allegory: the Letter of Aristeas and Philo. (6) Identity: food marks Israel off from the nations (20:24–26). (7) Decree: the rabbis' chukkim, obeyed because God gave them (Sifra on 20:26).

a: chews the cud
p: An allowed land animal needs both a fully split hoof and cud-chewing. Deuteronomy 14 names ten examples.
b: Both signs are needed: hooves split right through into two toes, and chewing the cud, bringing food back up to chew again. That allows cattle, sheep, goats and the wild deer, gazelles and ibex named in Deuteronomy 14:4–5, the animals of herding peoples. The rule excludes animals that eat flesh, which have paws (11:27). The rabbis added that any animal with both signs is allowed, even if not named, and observed that only four animals have one sign without the other, the four named in 11:4–7 (Talmud, Chullin 59a).

a: The rock hyrax chews the cud
t: Does the hare chew the cud?
p: Hyraxes and hares are not true ruminants. But they move their jaws constantly, and hares re-eat food.
b: Critics point out that the hyrax (KJV "coney," a small rock-dwelling animal) and the hare do not have the four-chambered stomach of true cud-chewers. Defenders reply that the Hebrew "brings up the cud" describes what an observer sees: both animals chew constantly with a sideways motion, and hares eat their own soft droppings to digest food a second time, which works much like cud-chewing. The law was written to be applied by herders, not by biologists, and its categories are those of ordinary sight, like "bird" in 11:19.

a: The pig
p: Pig bones are nearly absent from early Israelite highland villages, but common at Philistine sites.
b: Archaeologists have found that pig bones are very rare in the hill villages of Iron Age I (about 1200–1000 BC) usually identified as early Israel, while they are common in Philistine cities on the coast and in some earlier Canaanite towns. Israel Finkelstein and others argue that avoiding pork was already a mark of identity before the laws were written down. Others explain it by environment: pigs need water and shade and do poorly in dry hill country (Marvin Harris). In the Maccabean crisis Jews were forced to eat pork and some died rather than do it (2 Maccabees 6:18–7:42), which made the pig a symbol of loyalty.
r: Deuteronomy 14:8; Isaiah 65:4; Isaiah 66:17; 1 Maccabees 1:47; 2 Maccabees 6:18–31; Luke 15:15–16

a: anything in the seas or the streams that has fins and scales
p: No shellfish, shark, catfish or eel. Douglas saw creatures that do not "swim properly" excluded.
b: Water creatures need both fins and scales. That leaves out shellfish, crabs and lobsters, catfish, eels, sharks and whales. Mary Douglas argued that the clean fish are those that fit the ordinary picture of a sea creature, while those that crawl on the bottom or lack scales blur the categories. The rabbis noted that every fish with scales also has fins (Mishnah Niddah 6:9). The word sheqets, "detestable" (11:10), is used only of animals, while to'evah ("abomination") is used in Deuteronomy 14:3 and for sins in 18:22.

a: Among the birds, you are to treat these as detestable
p: No signs are given for birds, only a list, and many of the Hebrew names cannot be identified for sure.
b: Unlike land and water animals, birds have no test, just a list of about twenty. The names are uncertain, and English Bibles differ widely: nesher may be an eagle or the griffon vulture (Micah 1:16 speaks of its bald head); the "ostrich" (bat hayya'anah) may be an owl. Most that can be identified eat flesh or carrion, which led Ramban and the Letter of Aristeas to see a lesson against violence: Israel should not take in the nature of predators. The rabbis later gave signs of their own and in practice allowed only birds with a tradition of being eaten (Mishnah Chullin 3:6).

a: the bat
p: The Hebrew 'of means any "flying thing," not "bird" in the modern scientific sense.
b: Critics sometimes say the Bible calls the bat a bird. But the heading word 'of (11:13) means "winged, flying creature," from the verb "to fly," and covers flying insects too (11:20). Ancient categories grouped animals by how they move and where they live, not by how they reproduce. Calling a bat a 'of is no more an error than calling a whale a "fish" in old English. The modern "bird" class does not exist in the Hebrew.

a: any kind of locust
p: Four kinds of locust and grasshopper are allowed. John the Baptist lived on locusts and wild honey.
b: Locusts were (and in parts of the Near East still are) eaten roasted, boiled or dried. Assyrian palace reliefs show servants carrying locusts on skewers to a royal banquet. John the Baptist ate "locusts and wild honey" (Mark 1:6), clean food from the wilderness. Yemenite and some North African Jewish communities kept a tradition of which locusts were permitted; most others stopped eating them because the four Hebrew names could no longer be identified with certainty. The Dead Sea Scrolls' Damascus Document gives rules for cooking them (12:14–15).

a: Whoever touches their dead bodies will be unclean until evening.
p: The lightest uncleanness: wait until sunset and wash. Why did death make one unclean at all?
b: Touching the carcass of an unclean animal, or carrying it, makes a person unclean "until the evening": he must wash his clothes and wait for sunset (11:25). Living unclean animals do not make anyone unclean; only dead ones do. Milgrom saw a pattern across chapters 11–15: uncleanness is tied to death and the loss of life (corpses, blood, semen, the wasting skin of chapter 13). Holiness is life, so the things of death must be kept from the sanctuary. Others (Hyam Maccoby, Jonathan Klawans) accept the death link in part, but stress that the system also marks the boundaries of Israel's worship. Either way, uncleanness here is a temporary state, not a moral failure (see 5:2).

a: a spring or a cistern that collects water
p: Water in the ground does not become unclean. The rabbis built the ritual bath, the mikveh, on this verse.
b: A pot that a dead mouse falls into is unclean (11:33), but a spring or a cistern stays clean. The Hebrew miqveh mayim, "gathering of water," gave its name to the Jewish ritual bath, the mikveh. The rabbis ruled that a valid immersion pool must hold natural water, rain or spring, not water drawn in vessels, and of a set minimum size (Mishnah Mikvaot). Hundreds of stepped pools from the time of Jesus have been found in Jerusalem, at Qumran and elsewhere. Jeremiah calls God "the hope (miqveh) of Israel" and "the spring of living water" (Jeremiah 17:13), a pun Rabbi Akiva used (Mishnah Yoma 8:9).

a: crawls on its belly
p: The same word as the snake's curse in Genesis 3:14. In scrolls its letter vav is written large.
b: Gachon, "belly," appears only here and in the curse on the snake: "On your belly you will crawl, and dust you will eat" (Genesis 3:14). Creatures that move this way are kept off Israel's table. The Hebrew letter vav in this word is written oversized in Torah scrolls, marking it, by an old count, as the middle letter of the Torah (see 10:16). Genesis 1 also groups creatures by how they move: the "creeping things" (Genesis 1:24–25), the same word as "swarming things" here.

a: Keep yourselves holy, and be holy, for I am holy.
p: The book's motto first appears here, at the table. Peter quotes it; Jesus recasts it.
b: This is the first time the great command appears; it returns at 19:2, 20:7 and 20:26. It comes at an unexpected place, the menu, as if to say holiness reaches the kitchen. The rabbis built the imitation of God on several verses: "As he is gracious and merciful, so you be gracious and merciful" (Talmud, Shabbat 133b, on Exodus 15:2; compare Sifra on Leviticus 19:2). Peter quotes it to Christians: "as the one who called you is holy, be holy yourselves in all you do, because it is written, 'You will be holy, because I am holy'" (1 Peter 1:15–16). Jesus' "So you are to be perfect, the way your heavenly Father is perfect" (Matthew 5:48) and "Become compassionate, the way your Father is compassionate" (Luke 6:36) take up the pattern.
orig: וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אָנִי (vihyitem qedoshim ki qadosh ani)

a: who brought you up from the land of Egypt
t: Brought up, not just brought out
p: Usually God "brought out" Israel from Egypt. Here he "brought up." The rabbis heard a lift in rank.
b: Most exodus formulas say God "brought you out" (hotseti, as in 19:36). Here the verb is hama'aleh, "who brought up." The Talmud (Bava Metzia 61b) has God say: "Had I brought Israel up from Egypt only for this, that they not defile themselves with creeping things, it would be enough," and finds in "brought up" a raising of their status. The exodus is given as the reason for the food laws: the God who freed Israel has a right to shape its daily life.

a: the creatures that may be eaten from those that may not be eaten
t: Do the food laws still apply?
p: Jews keep them as covenant law. Most Christians read Mark 7:19 and Acts 10 as setting them aside. Some disagree.
b: In Judaism these laws remain binding, the core of kashrut. In the New Testament, Mark adds to Jesus' saying about what defiles a person: "making all foods clean" (Mark 7:19). Most Christians read this, with Peter's vision of unclean animals (Acts 10:9–16) and Paul's "nothing is unclean of itself" (Romans 14:14; also Colossians 2:16–17), as ending the food laws for the church. Others, including many Messianic Jews and scholars such as Daniel Boyarin and David Rudolph, argue that Mark 7 is about eating with unwashed hands, not about forbidden animals, and that Peter's vision is explained as being about people: "to me God has shown that no human being is to be called common or unclean" (Acts 10:28). The Byzantine text of Mark 7:19 reads the participle so that it refers to the latrine, not to Jesus.

a: When a woman yields seed and bears a male
p: The verb is the causative of "sow": the woman "produces seed." The rabbis built a theory of conception on it.
b: Tazria is a form of zara, "sow," so literally "yields seed" or "produces seed." Most translations simply say "conceives." Genesis 1:11–12 uses the same verb for plants "yielding seed." The Talmud builds on it a saying that if the woman "yields seed" first, the child will be a boy (Niddah 31a), an ancient theory of conception, not science. The chapter gives its name to the Torah portion Tazria.

a: she will be unclean seven days
