p: Not because birth or sex is sinful. Most scholars point to the loss of blood, the stuff of life.
b: The text does not say why. Readings: (1) Blood loss: blood is life (17:11), and the flow after birth, like the monthly flow, marks a loss of life-force (Milgrom, Wenham). (2) Birth as a boundary: a passage between life and death, which anthropologists find surrounded with taboos in many cultures. (3) The Talmud's guess: in the pains of labor a woman swears never to sleep with her husband again, so she brings an offering for the rash oath (Niddah 31b). (4) Some feminist critics see in it a male system that treats female bodies as dangerous. The text, though, calls the birth itself nothing wrong, and the offering is for cleansing. Hannah's and Mary's joy at their sons' births (1 Samuel 2:1; Luke 1:46) sits beside these laws.

a: On the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin is to be circumcised.
p: The rule given to Abraham is repeated in the middle of a purity law. It overrides even the Sabbath.
b: God told Abraham, "Every male among you, generation after generation, is to be circumcised at eight days old" (Genesis 17:12). The law sits here because the mother's first week of uncleanness ends when her son's covenant begins. The rabbis ruled that circumcision on the eighth day is done even on a Sabbath (Mishnah Shabbat 19:2), and Jesus uses this to defend healing on the Sabbath (John 7:22–23). Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), and so was Paul (Philippians 3:5).
r: Genesis 17:10–14; Genesis 21:4; Luke 1:59; Luke 2:21; John 7:22–23; Philippians 3:5

a: in her blood purifying
p: After the first week the woman is in a milder state: she may not touch holy things, but she is not fully unclean.
b: The forty days fall into two stages. The first seven (for a boy) are like the monthly flow: she makes things she touches unclean (15:19–24). The next thirty-three are "the blood of purifying": she still bleeds, but this blood is treated as clean for ordinary life; she simply may not touch holy food or enter the sanctuary. The rabbis called it "pure blood" (Mishnah Niddah 4:3). In later practice many Jewish communities, following a stricter custom, ceased to observe the distinction. In the Jesus story, Mary's "days of purification" end when she comes to the temple (Luke 2:22).

a: If she bears a female child, she will be unclean two weeks
p: Fourteen and sixty-six days for a girl, seven and thirty-three for a boy. Explanations differ sharply.
b: The text gives no reason. (1) Medical: the Hippocratic treatise On the Nature of the Child says the flow after birth lasts about thirty days for a boy and forty-two for a girl, and Aristotle thought a female child developed more slowly. (2) Creation: the oldest Jewish explanation, in Jubilees 3:8–14, says Adam was brought into Eden on the fortieth day after he was made, and Eve on the eightieth. (3) The Talmud (Niddah 31b) says a son's birth brings joy, so the mother regrets her oath of labor sooner. (4) Some modern scholars suggest the newborn girl, a future mother, is counted too. (5) Many readers, Jewish and Christian, see it as reflecting the lower status of women in that society, and say so plainly. The offerings, though, are the same for a son or a daughter (12:6).

a: a young dove or a turtledove for a sin offering
t: A sin offering for giving birth?
p: She has not sinned. The hatta't here purifies (see 4:3). The Talmud suggested a reason anyway.
b: This verse is one of the strongest arguments for calling the hatta't a "purification offering" (see 4:3): bearing a child is a blessing (Genesis 1:28; Psalm 127:3), not a sin. Still, the old name led many readers to ask what her sin was, and the Talmud's answer was the rash oath of labor (12:2). Christian writers asked why Mary, the mother of Jesus, needed such an offering. Most answered that she kept the law out of obedience, not because she needed cleansing. The order differs from usual: the burnt offering is named first, perhaps because it is the larger gift.

a: If she cannot afford a sheep
p: Mary and Joseph bring "a pair of turtledoves or two young doves": the offering of the poor.
b: Luke tells that when the days of purification were over, Mary and Joseph took Jesus to Jerusalem "to give a sacrifice, as the law of the Lord says: 'a pair of turtledoves or two young doves'" (Luke 2:24). Luke quotes this verse, the offering for one who cannot afford a lamb. Christian writers from early on drew the lesson that the family was poor, and that the Lamb of God came into the world through a mother who could not afford a lamb. The same verse is the root of the old church feast of the Purification of Mary, or Candlemas, on February 2, forty days after Christmas.

a: a mark of skin disease
p: Tsara'at is not Hansen's disease. It is a scaly, flaking condition that also strikes cloth and walls.
b: Older Bibles say "leprosy." But the symptoms here (white or reddish patches, flaking skin, white hair in the spot, "raw flesh") do not match Hansen's disease, which causes numbness, damaged nerves and loss of fingers, none of which are mentioned. Some cases heal in a week (13:6). Tsara'at also appears in cloth (13:47) and houses (14:34). The Greek translation used lepra, which meant scaly skin, perhaps psoriasis; the modern disease got the name later. E. V. Hulse, a medical doctor, argued it covered conditions such as psoriasis, fungal infections and eczema. Skeletons from India show Hansen's disease by about 2000 BC, but it is not attested in Egypt or the Levant before the Hellenistic period. The Plain English says "skin disease" to avoid the misleading word.

a: He is to be brought to Aaron the priest
p: The priest diagnoses and declares. He gives no treatment, no medicine and no prayer for healing.
b: Strikingly, the chapter never tells the priest to treat the disease. There are no ointments, spells or prayers, unlike Babylonian and Egyptian medical texts, where priests and healers used both. The priest's work is to look, to wait, and to declare a person's status, clean or unclean. Healing is left to God (14:3). In Mesopotamia the ashipu was an exorcist-healer; Israel's priest is neither. Later, Jesus touches a man with skin disease, heals him, and then sends him to the priest for the declaration (Mark 1:40–44).

a: it is a mark of skin disease
t: Clothed in disease like a garment
p: Babylonian boundary stones curse enemies with skin disease and banishment. Israel's law does not curse.
b: Babylonian kudurru stones, which marked property lines, often end with curses: may the moon god "clothe his body with leprosy (saharshubbu) as with a garment," so that he roams outside the city like a wild ass. In Mesopotamia this skin disease was a sign of divine anger and meant expulsion. Israel shares the idea of exclusion (13:46) and sometimes links the disease to sin (Numbers 12:10; 2 Kings 5:27), but Leviticus 13 never calls it punishment and never mentions demons. Verdict: a common Near Eastern fear of skin disease, handled in Leviticus as a matter of ritual status.

a: he is to declare him unclean
p: The verb means "pronounce unclean." Until the priest speaks, the person is not unclean.
b: Timme'o is a declarative form: "he shall pronounce him unclean." The rabbis drew out the force of this: only a priest can declare, even if a learned non-priest does the examining and tells the priest what to say (Mishnah Negaim 3:1). Until the priest speaks, the person and his house are not unclean, which is why the house is emptied before the priest goes in (14:36). Uncleanness is a legal status, not just a medical fact.

a: the priest is to shut the person with the mark away for seven days
p: Seven days of isolation, then a second look. The point is to see whether the spot spreads.
b: Hisgir, "shut up, close in," is the word for keeping the person apart while waiting to see what the mark does. It looks like modern quarantine, and in times of epidemic many have read it that way. But the chapter never mentions catching the disease from others, and the rabbis exempted non-Jews (Mishnah Negaim 3:1) and let the inspection be put off for a bridegroom or during a festival (3:2), which would make little sense if contagion were the concern. The waiting is a test: a mark that spreads shows itself, one that fades is "only a rash."

a: He has turned all white, and he is clean.
p: A man covered from head to foot is declared clean. Interpreters have puzzled and preached on it.
b: This is the chapter's paradox: a spot is unclean, but total whiteness is clean, unless raw flesh appears (13:14). Milgrom explains that when the whole skin has turned white and flaky, the disease has run its course and new skin is forming; the danger signal is raw, open flesh. The rabbis drew a saying about the end of days: the son of David will come only when the whole kingdom has turned to heresy, "all of it turned white, he is clean" (Talmud, Sanhedrin 97a). Christian preachers made it a picture of the sinner who confesses he is wholly sinful and so is made clean (compare Luke 18:13–14). These applications are sermons, not the text's meaning.

a: is to wear torn clothes and let his hair hang loose
p: Torn clothes, loose hair and a covered lip are the signs of mourning. He grieves as if for himself.
b: These are the marks of mourning for the dead (10:6; Ezekiel 24:17). The person with skin disease mourns, in a sense, for himself, since his body looks like it is wasting toward death. Aaron pleads for Miriam: "Please do not let her be like the dead, like one who comes out of his mother's womb with half his flesh eaten away" (Numbers 12:12). Josephus says such people were treated "as though dead" (Antiquities 3.264). He must call out "Unclean! Unclean!" so others can keep away. Lamentations uses the same cry for the exiles: "'Keep away, unclean!' people called out to them" (Lamentations 4:15). The ten men in Luke "stood at a distance" and called to Jesus (Luke 17:12–13).

a: He is to live alone
p: The rabbis linked skin disease to slander: metsora, "diseased," sounds like motsi ra, "one who spreads evil."
b: Leviticus does not say why tsara'at strikes. But in the stories it often follows a sin: Miriam's speech against Moses (Numbers 12:1–10), Gehazi's greed (2 Kings 5:27), Uzziah's pride (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The rabbis heard in metsora the phrase motsi shem ra, "one who brings out a bad name," and taught that skin disease came for slander and gossip (lashon hara), listing also bloodshed, false oaths, sexual sin, pride, theft and stinginess (Talmud, Arakhin 15b–16a). Why must he live alone? "He separated husband from wife and friend from friend, so he is separated" (Arakhin 16b). Many modern readers note that the text itself names no sin.

a: his home is to be outside the camp
p: Lepers lived outside towns into Jesus' day. Jesus touched one, a shocking act in light of this law.
b: People with skin disease were sent "outside the camp" (Numbers 5:2–3), later outside the city: four such men sat at the gate of Samaria (2 Kings 7:3), and King Uzziah lived in "a separate house" (2 Kings 15:5). Jesus, when a man with skin disease knelt before him, "reached out his hand and touched him" and he was made clean (Mark 1:40–42). Instead of the uncleanness passing to Jesus, the cleanness passed to the man. Jesus then told him to show himself to the priest and offer what Moses commanded (Mark 1:44; see chapter 14). Hebrews calls believers to go to Jesus "outside the camp" (Hebrews 13:13).
r: Numbers 5:2–4; Numbers 12:14–15; 2 Kings 7:3; 2 Kings 15:5; Mark 1:40–45; Luke 17:12–19; Hebrews 13:12–13

a: a mark of mold
p: Hebrew uses the same word, tsara'at, for marks on skin, cloth and walls. English needs two words.
b: The Hebrew simply speaks of "a mark of tsara'at" in a garment, and later in a house (14:34). English Bibles say "mildew," "mold" or "fungus," since no one thinks cloth catches a human disease. The Plain English says "mold" but readers should know that the Hebrew word is the same as in 13:2. That suggests tsara'at named a kind of appearance, a spreading, flaking or discolored surface, rather than a disease in the modern sense (Baden and Moss). Greenish and reddish spots on wool, linen or leather match common molds.

a: The priest is to go outside the camp and examine him.
p: The healed person cannot come in until declared clean, so the priest must go out to him.
b: The rite begins with the priest leaving the camp to find the outcast where he lives. Only after the first stage may the person come in, and only on the eighth day may he come to the tent. Jesus sent the healed man, "Go and let the priest see you. Then bring for your cleansing what Moses ordered" (Mark 1:44), and the ten, "Go and let the priests see you" (Luke 17:14). The law assumes healing comes from God; the priest only confirms it.

a: two clean live birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn and hyssop
p: The same three things are burned with the red heifer for the water that cleanses from death (Numbers 19:6).
b: Cedar is long-lasting wood that resists rot; scarlet yarn is red, the color of blood and life; hyssop is a small bushy plant used as a sprinkler (Exodus 12:22). The same set is used in the red heifer rite, which cleanses from contact with the dead (Numbers 19:6). Together they seem to stand for life overcoming death. The healed person was, in effect, returning from the dead (13:45). David prays, "Take away my sin with hyssop" (Psalm 51:7), and a hyssop branch held up the sponge to Jesus at the cross (John 19:29). Solomon's wisdom ran "from the cedar ... to the hyssop" (1 Kings 4:33), from greatest to least.
r: 14:6; 14:49–52; Exodus 12:22; Numbers 19:6; Numbers 19:18; 1 Kings 4:33; Psalm 51:7; John 19:29; Hebrews 9:19

a: over fresh water
p: Mayim chayyim is flowing water from a spring or stream. The phrase becomes a picture of God's life.
b: "Living water" means running water, not water standing in a jar (15:13; Numbers 19:17). The blood of the slain bird drips into a clay pot of such water. The phrase grows in the Bible into a picture of God himself: "me they have left, the spring of living water" (Jeremiah 2:13). Zechariah sees living water flowing out from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8). Jesus offers the Samaritan woman "living water" (John 4:10) and says of the one who believes in him, "Out of his belly rivers of living water will flow" (John 7:38).
r: 14:50–52; 15:13; Numbers 19:17; Jeremiah 2:13; Jeremiah 17:13; Zechariah 14:8; John 4:10–14; John 7:38

a: Then he is to set the live bird free over the open field.
p: Like the goat for Azazel, a living creature carries something away. Hittite rites send off animals too.
b: One bird dies; the other, dipped in its blood, is set free to fly away over the open country. Most scholars think it carries the uncleanness away, as the goat for Azazel carries sins into the wilderness (16:21–22; compare 14:53, done for a house). Hittite and Mesopotamian rituals also sent off birds, animals or figurines to carry evil out of a community (David P. Wright). Israel's rite has no demon and no spell: it is God who heals, and the priest who declares. Some Christian interpreters have seen in the two birds a picture of Christ's death and resurrection, the living bird dipped in the blood of the slain one.

a: shave off all his hair
p: Shaved bare, washed and changed, the healed person starts over, like the Levites at their dedication.
b: Shaving all hair is done also by Levites at their dedication (Numbers 8:7) and by a Nazirite who has been made unclean by a dead body (Numbers 6:9). The healed person comes out hairless like a newborn. Mary Douglas and others read the rite as a rebirth: the person who was counted as dead (13:45) is reborn into the community in stages, first into the camp, then after seven days to his own tent, then on the eighth day before the LORD. 2 Kings 5:14 says Naaman's flesh came back "like the flesh of a young lad."

a: present it as a guilt offering
p: A guilt offering is for sacrilege. Its presence here suggests a fear that the disease came from wronging the holy.
b: The healed person brings a guilt offering (asham), which elsewhere repays sacrilege against holy things (5:14–16). Milgrom suggested that the offering covers the possibility that the person had, knowingly or not, committed sacrilege, since skin disease was known as a punishment for it (Uzziah, 2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Others think it simply makes up to God for the offerings and service the person could not bring while banished. Its blood, rather than the sin offering's, is put on the ear, thumb and toe.

a: on the lobe of the right ear of the person being cleansed
p: The healed outcast receives the same marks as Aaron at his ordination (8:23–24).
b: Blood on the right ear, thumb and big toe, and then oil on the same spots (14:17), repeat the rite of Aaron's ordination (8:23–24, 30). The person who was cut off from the community is brought back with the honors of a priest. Gordon Wenham and others call this a kind of re-consecration: he too belongs to a "kingdom of priests" (Exodus 19:6). The rest of the oil goes on his head (14:18), as anointing oil went on Aaron's (8:12).

a: There I may put a mark of mold in a house in the land you hold.
p: God says "I put" it. A midrash says the Canaanites hid gold in their walls, and the mold made Israel find it.
b: This law looks forward to settled life in Canaan, in houses of stone and plaster. God speaks of putting the mark himself. Rashi, following Leviticus Rabbah 17:6, saw it as good news: the Canaanites had hidden gold in the walls of their houses during the forty years Israel was in the wilderness, and tearing out the marked stones revealed the treasure. Other rabbis saw the mold as a warning for stinginess: the owner who told neighbors he had nothing to lend would have to empty his house for all to see (Talmud, Arakhin 16a). Modern scholars read it as a practical law about dangerous mold in damp walls, given religious form.

a: The priest is to order the house to be emptied before he goes in
p: Things are carried out before the priest declares. Uncleanness begins with the priest's word.
b: Before the priest looks, everything is taken out of the house, so that the contents will not be declared unclean along with the walls. This shows that uncleanness here starts at the declaration, not at the first appearance of the mold (see 13:3). The rabbis remarked, "The Torah has pity on a person's property": the main loss would be clay pots, which can only be broken (Mishnah Negaim 12:5; Rashi). Things could be rescued even if the house could not.

a: The house is to be torn down
p: One rabbinic opinion says a house with tsara'at never existed: the law was given to be studied.
b: A house in which the mark comes back is pulled down stone by stone and carried to an unclean place. Some rabbis taught that such a case "never happened and never will happen," because the legal conditions were so strict, and asked: "Why was it written? So that you may study it and receive a reward." Others answered that a ruin of such a house was known "near Gaza" (Tosefta Negaim 6:1; Talmud, Sanhedrin 71a). The discussion shows how the rabbis valued study of the law for its own sake (compare 7:37).

a: To cleanse the house from sin
p: The same verb as for the altar (8:15). Atonement is made for a house (14:53), which cannot sin.
b: Lechatte is the "un-sinning" verb of 8:15, and 14:53 says "he will make atonement for the house." A house cannot do wrong, so here both terms must mean removing pollution, not forgiving guilt. This is one of Milgrom's main proofs that kipper can mean "purge" (see 1:4). The same two birds, cedar, scarlet and hyssop are used as for a person (14:4–7), so the house and the healed person go through the same cleansing.

a: a discharge from his body
p: Basar, "flesh," is here a polite word for the sexual organ. The discharge is a flow from it.
b: Basar usually means flesh or body, but here (and in Ezekiel 16:26; 23:20) it is a modest way to name the male organ. The man with a zov, a "flow," has a running discharge, perhaps gonorrhea or another infection, and the rabbis distinguished it carefully from semen (Mishnah Zavim 2:2). He becomes a zav, "one who flows," and his uncleanness spreads to what he lies or sits on. The chapter is built in mirror form: abnormal male flow (15:2–15), normal male emission (15:16–18), normal female flow (15:19–24), abnormal female flow (15:25–30).

a: without first rinsing his hands in water
p: Rinsing the hands stops the man's touch from passing uncleanness. Later Jews made handwashing a rule.
b: If the man with a discharge rinses his hands, his touch does not pass on uncleanness. The rabbis took this as one of the roots of ritual handwashing before eating, which was widely practiced by Jesus' time. Mark 7:1–5 tells of Pharisees who "do not eat unless they wash their hands," asking why Jesus' disciples ate "with common hands," that is, unwashed ones. Jesus' answer, that what defiles comes from the heart, became the setting for Mark's comment on foods (see 11:47).

a: When a man has an emission of seed
p: Normal sex and emissions make a person unclean only until evening. No sin, only distance from holy things.
b: A man who has an emission of seed is unclean until evening and must wash; so must the woman after intercourse (15:18). Before meeting God at Sinai the people were told, "Do not come near a woman" (Exodus 19:15), and David's men could eat the holy bread only if they had "kept from women" (1 Samuel 21:4–5). Milgrom tied this to the life-and-death pattern: seed is life lost from the body. Others see a simpler point: sex belongs to ordinary life and is kept apart from the sanctuary. The law nowhere calls sex wrong; Genesis 1:28 commands it.

a: both of them are to bathe in water
p: Some neighboring cults had sacred sex. Herodotus says only Egyptians and Greeks kept it out of temples.
b: This rule puts a barrier between sex and the holy place. The Greek historian Herodotus wrote that the Egyptians were the first to forbid intercourse in temples and to require washing after it before entering one, and that almost all other peoples except the Greeks did otherwise (Histories 2.64). How widespread "sacred prostitution" really was in the ancient Near East is now hotly debated, and many scholars doubt it existed as an institution. Still, Israel's law clearly separates the bed from the altar, and the prophets condemn mixing the two (Hosea 4:13–14; Amos 2:7).

a: she is to be in her separation for seven days
p: A monthly week of ritual impurity. Not a sin, not a curse, but later used as a picture of moral filth.
b: Niddah probably comes from a root meaning "put apart, expel" (the blood is expelled; or she is set apart). For seven days a woman is unclean: whoever touches her or her bed is unclean until evening. Nothing calls her sinful, and no offering is required for a normal period. Yet the prophets turned niddah into a metaphor for vile sin (Ezekiel 36:17; Lamentations 1:17; Ezra 9:11), and in some later cultures the laws were used to shame women. Charlotte Fonrobert and others have traced how rabbinic and Christian writers reshaped the law. Rachel Adler first presented the practice as a meditation on life and death (1972), then rejected that view as hiding a hierarchy (1993). Readers today disagree.

a: Anything she lies on during her separation will be unclean
t: Niddah in Jewish and Christian practice
p: Rabbinic law kept the rules in the home; the church debated them and mostly let them go.
b: After the Temple fell, most purity laws lapsed, but rabbinic law kept the ban on marital relations during and after the period (18:19), adding a further seven "clean days" and immersion in a mikveh (Talmud, Niddah 66a). This "family purity" is still practiced in Orthodox Judaism, and many women describe it as a source of dignity, others as a burden. In the church, some early writers barred menstruating women from communion, but Pope Gregory the Great wrote to Augustine of Canterbury that a woman should not be forbidden to enter church or receive communion during her period (as reported by Bede, Ecclesiastical History 1.27), and that view largely prevailed in the West.

a: If a man lies with her
t: Seven days here, cut off in chapter 20?
p: Here the man is unclean seven days. Leviticus 18:19 and 20:18 forbid the act and threaten being cut off.
b: This verse treats intercourse during the period as making the man unclean for seven days, with no other penalty. But 18:19 forbids it, and 20:18 threatens both with being "cut off." The rabbis harmonized the two: 15:24 covers a case where the period began during intercourse or was unknown, while chapters 18 and 20 cover a knowing act. Critical scholars often see two layers: the Priestly writers of 11–16, concerned with ritual impurity, and the Holiness writers of 17–26, who turned it into a moral prohibition (Israel Knohl, Milgrom).

a: A woman may have a flow of blood for many days
p: A woman with this condition for twelve years touched Jesus' cloak. Instead of uncleanness passing, power went out.
b: This law describes a woman whose bleeding goes on beyond her normal period. She is unclean as long as it lasts, and so is anything she lies or sits on. The Gospels tell of a woman "who had had a flow of blood twelve years long" (Mark 5:25). By this law she had been unable to touch others without passing on uncleanness for all that time. She touched the edge of Jesus' cloak, perhaps its tassel (Numbers 15:38), and was healed. Jesus, instead of being made unclean, felt that "power had gone out of him" and called her "Daughter" (Mark 5:30–34). The story turns this verse around.

a: so that they do not die in their uncleanness by making my tabernacle, which is among them, unclean
p: The real danger of uncleanness: it pollutes God's dwelling. Milgrom thought it did so from a distance.
b: Here is the purpose of chapters 11–15: uncleanness, left untreated, pollutes "my tabernacle, which is among them." Jacob Milgrom argued that impurity works like an airborne stain that reaches the sanctuary from anywhere in the camp, building up until God would leave, an idea he compared to Oscar Wilde's Picture of Dorian Gray, whose portrait grows ugly with each sin. The sin offering and the Day of Atonement remove the build-up (16:16). Roy Gane argues instead that the evil reaches the sanctuary through the purification offerings themselves, which carry it from the offerer to the sanctuary, and is removed on the Day of Atonement. Hyam Maccoby doubts that sin pollutes from a distance at all. Ezekiel sees the glory leave a defiled temple (Ezekiel 10:18–19).

a: after the death of Aaron's two sons
p: Chapter 16 picks up from chapter 10. The purity laws between were placed there for a reason.
b: This verse links the Day of Atonement to Nadab and Abihu (10:1–2). The rule that follows, "not at just any time," answers their fatal approach. Chapters 11–15 interrupt the story. Many think the placement is deliberate: after teaching how impurity arises (11–15), the book shows how the sanctuary is cleansed of it (16). Others see the purity laws as a later insertion. The Greek translation adds that they died "when they brought strange fire" (see the variant). Rashi compares a doctor warning a patient: "Do not lie in a damp place, or you will die like so-and-so."

a: he must not come at just any time into the holy place behind the veil
p: Only the high priest, only on this day, only with blood and incense, could enter the inner room.
b: Here "the holy place behind the veil" means the inner room, the most holy place, where the ark stood. Aaron may not come in whenever he likes. The date is fixed in 16:29 and 16:34, "once a year." Hebrews: "into the second room the high priest alone goes, once a year, and never without blood" (Hebrews 9:7). Philo wrote that if the high priest went in on any other day, or even entered twice on that day, he would die (Embassy to Gaius 307). The Mishnah says he went in four times on the day itself, with incense and with blood (Yoma 5:1–4; 7:4).

a: For I will appear in the cloud over the atonement lid.
p: God's cloud of glory, or the cloud of incense (16:13)? The question split Pharisees and Sadducees.
b: The "cloud" may be God's own cloud of glory, or the incense smoke of 16:13. The answer mattered in practice. The Sadducees, the priestly party, held that the high priest must put the incense on the coals before he went inside, so that he would enter in a cloud. The Pharisees held that he lit it inside, as 16:13 says. The Talmud tells of a Sadducee high priest who did it his way and died soon after (Yoma 19b; Tosefta Yoma 1:8), and the Mishnah says the high priest was made to swear the night before that he would follow the Pharisees' ruling (Yoma 1:5). On the atonement lid (kapporet) see the note on Exodus 25:17.

a: He is to put on a holy linen tunic
p: On this day the high priest takes off his gold and colored robes and wears plain white linen.
b: Usually the high priest wore the gold ephod, breastpiece and blue robe (Exodus 28). To enter the inner room he wears only simple linen, like an ordinary priest, or like an angel: Ezekiel and Daniel see heavenly beings "clothed in linen" (Ezekiel 9:2; Daniel 10:5), and Revelation's angels wear it (Revelation 15:6). The rabbis gave another reason: gold recalls the golden calf, and "an accuser cannot become a defender" (Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 26a). Many Christians saw in it Christ laying aside his glory (Philippians 2:7). The Mishnah says he changed clothes five times that day and bathed each time (Yoma 3:3).

a: one lot for the LORD and the other lot for Azazel
p: A demon of the desert? A cliff? "The goat that goes away"? Or "complete removal"? Four views.
b: Azazel appears only in this chapter. (1) A demon of the wilderness, matching "for the LORD" with a personal name. In 1 Enoch (third century BC) Azazel is a fallen angel bound in the desert (1 Enoch 10:4–8). Ramban said the goat was a gift to the ruler of desolate places, given at God's command, not worship (compare 17:7). Milgrom thinks a demon was once meant but the rite strips it of power. (2) A place: a rugged cliff, the rabbis' view (Talmud, Yoma 67b; Rashi). (3) "The goat that goes away" (ez azel): the Greek apopompaios, "sent away," the Latin caper emissarius, and Tyndale's 1530 coinage "scapegoat." (4) "For complete removal," from an Arabic root (some modern scholars). The Plain English keeps the name.

a: Aaron is to cast lots for the two goats
t: The lots and the scarlet thread
p: The Talmud says that in the Temple's last forty years the signs went wrong.
b: The Mishnah describes two lots of boxwood, later gold, drawn from an urn, with the high priest placing them on the goats' heads (Yoma 3:9; 4:1). A strip of scarlet wool was tied to the goat for Azazel, and part of it to the cliff or the temple door; the tradition said it turned white when the people's sins were forgiven, recalling Isaiah 1:18, "though your sins are like scarlet, they will be white as snow" (Yoma 6:8; 67a). The Talmud says that in the forty years before the Temple fell in AD 70, the lot "for the LORD" no longer came up in the right hand and the thread no longer turned white (Yoma 39b). Some Christian writers saw a sign that atonement had moved to Christ.

a: by sending it away into the wilderness to Azazel
p: Hittite and Syrian rituals sent animals off with plague or guilt. Israel's version has no magic.
b: Rituals of "elimination" were widespread. In the Hittite plague ritual of Ashella, a ram decorated with colored wool was driven toward the enemy's land to carry the plague away. Texts from Ebla in Syria (about 2400 BC) describe a goat with a silver bracelet sent away to a wasteland before a royal wedding to purify the palace (Ida Zatelli). Greek cities drove out a human pharmakos in times of disaster. Verdict: Israel shares a real, old Near Eastern form, but in Leviticus the goat carries the people's confessed sins, the high priest acts at God's command, and no god of the desert is fed or bribed. On the goat "to make atonement on it" see the note on 1:4: here the atonement is done by carrying away.

a: on the front of the atonement lid
p: The Greek word for the lid, hilasterion, is the word Paul uses for Christ in Romans 3:25.
b: Blood on and before the kapporet was the heart of the day. The Greek translation called the lid hilastērion, "place of atonement." Paul writes that God "put him forward as the place of atonement, through faith, by his blood" (Romans 3:25); the Greek behind "place of atonement" is hilastērion. Many scholars think he means that Christ is the new atonement lid, the place where God meets his people and sin is dealt with, set out in public rather than hidden behind a veil. Others take the word more generally as "atoning sacrifice" or "propitiation" (the KJV). Hebrews 9:5 uses the same word for the lid itself. Luther's German Bible gave English "mercy seat" through Tyndale.

a: So he will make atonement for the holy place, because of the uncleanness of the Israelites
p: The blood purges the sanctuary itself, inner room, tent and altar, of a year's accumulated pollution.
b: The day has two parts. First the blood of the bull and the goat cleans the holy place, the tent and the altar (16:14–19). Then the live goat carries the people's sins away (16:20–22). Milgrom saw in the first part the climax of his theory (15:31): the year's impurities and sins, even "rebellions" (pesha'im) for which no ordinary offering was allowed, have stained the sanctuary, and once a year it must be scrubbed clean, or God would leave. Roy Gane argues that the day also completes the forgiveness of the people, a second stage after their individual sin offerings. Hebrews applies the picture to heaven, where "the heavenly things themselves" needed "better sacrifices than these" (Hebrews 9:23).

a: he is to go out to the altar that is before the LORD
p: The rabbis said the golden incense altar inside the tent; many modern scholars say the bronze altar outside.
b: "The altar that is before the LORD" is sometimes the gold incense altar (4:7, 18), whose horns get blood once a year (Exodus 30:10). The Mishnah (Yoma 5:5) and Rashi take it that way: the high priest "goes out" from the inner room to the incense altar in the outer room. But "go out" more naturally means leaving the tent, and the listing "the holy place, the tent of meeting and the altar" (16:20, 33) suggests three zones. So Ibn Ezra, Milgrom and many others take it as the bronze altar in the courtyard. Either way all three areas of the sanctuary are cleansed.

a: confess over it all the guilty deeds and rebellions of the Israelites
p: The Mishnah gives the words, and says the people fell on their faces when they heard God's name spoken.
b: The three words for wrong, avon (guilt), pesha (rebellion) and hatta't (sin), are the three God promised to forgive: "forgiving guilt, rebellion and sin" (Exodus 34:7). The Mishnah gives the confession: "Please, O LORD, your people the house of Israel have done wrong, rebelled and sinned before you," ending with 16:30. Hearing the high priest speak the divine name in these confessions, "the priests and the people standing in the court fell on their faces and said, 'Blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom forever'" (Yoma 6:2). The synagogue's Yom Kippur service, the Avodah, still retells these scenes in poetry, and the people bow at those words.

a: in the care of a man standing ready
t: The man who led the goat
p: The Mishnah says a priest usually led it, along a road with booths, to a cliff twelve miles away.
b: Ish itti appears only here: a man "ready" or "appointed for the time." The Mishnah describes the scene in the Second Temple: Jews from Babylon, it says, would pull the goat's hair and shout, "Take and go!" A ramp was built so the goat could leave the temple quickly. Ten booths stood along the road, each a Sabbath-day's walk apart, with food and drink for the leader. At a cliff called Tsok he pushed the goat over backward, and signals were passed back to Jerusalem (Yoma 6:4–8). This was a later practice; Leviticus says only that the goat is let go in the wilderness (16:22).

a: The goat will carry all their guilty deeds on itself
p: "Carry guilt" is the phrase Isaiah uses for the servant. Christians saw the goat as a picture of Christ.
b: Nasa avon, "carry guilt," is used of God forgiving (Exodus 34:7), of priests bearing guilt (10:17), and of Isaiah's servant: "he bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12; 53:4). John the Baptist calls Jesus "the Lamb of God... the one who takes the world's sin away" (John 1:29). The Epistle of Barnabas (chapter 7) read both goats as Christ: the slain one his death, the cursed one, crowned with scarlet wool, his suffering, with the scarlet robe of the passion. Justin Martyr saw in the two goats Christ's two comings (Dialogue 40). Hebrews 13:12 sees Jesus suffering outside the gate like the offerings burned outside the camp.
r: 10:17; 16:27; Exodus 34:7; Isaiah 53:4–12; John 1:29; Hebrews 9:28; Hebrews 13:11–12; 1 Peter 2:24

a: On the tenth day of the seventh month
p: The tenth of Tishri, in September or October. Acts calls it simply "the Fast."
b: The seventh month, later called Tishri, falls in September or October. The Day of Atonement comes ten days after the start of the month (23:24, 27), the day now called Rosh Hashanah, and five days before the Feast of Booths. In Paul's voyage, sailing had become dangerous "since the Fast was already past" (Acts 27:9), which shows how widely the day marked the calendar. In Jewish practice it remains the holiest day of the year, a full day of fasting and prayer, ending with the blast of the shofar.

a: you are to humble yourselves
p: The Hebrew means to humble or press down one's self. It came to mean fasting and more.
b: Literally "you shall afflict your souls" (KJV). Isaiah 58:3 and Psalm 35:13 show that it meant fasting: "I humbled my soul with fasting." The Mishnah lists five things given up on the day: eating and drinking, washing, anointing with oil, wearing leather sandals, and marital relations (Yoma 8:1). The same day is set to start the year of release (25:9). Isaiah 58:3–7 insists that the fast God wants also means freeing the oppressed and feeding the hungry, words read in synagogues on Yom Kippur.

a: You will be clean from all your sins before the LORD.
t: Sins against God, sins against people
p: The Mishnah read this verse to mean the day atones only for sins "before the LORD," not wrongs to others.
b: The Hebrew word order allows a sharp reading, and the Mishnah takes it: "'From all your sins before the LORD you will be clean': for wrongs between a person and God, the Day of Atonement atones; for wrongs between a person and his neighbor, the Day of Atonement does not atone until he has made peace with his neighbor" (Yoma 8:9, Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah). The same passage ends with Rabbi Akiva: "Happy are you, Israel! Before whom are you made clean, and who makes you clean? Your Father in heaven," quoting Ezekiel 36:25. Compare the order of repayment before offering in 6:5.

a: The priest who is anointed and whose hand is filled to serve as priest in his father's place
p: The rite was for every high priest to come. What happened when there was no temple?
b: The law is for all time, carried on by each high priest in turn. When the Temple fell in AD 70, Judaism lost the rite. Avot de Rabbi Natan tells that Rabbi Joshua wept at the ruins, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai told him, "We have another atonement as good as this: deeds of loving-kindness," as it is said in Hosea: "Loyal love is what I want, not sacrifice" (Hosea 6:6). Yom Kippur continued as a day of fasting, prayer, confession and repentance. Christians read Hebrews 7–10: Jesus is the high priest who entered "once for all" into the true holy place "with his own blood" (Hebrews 9:12). See the chapter page.

a: atonement is to be made once a year for the Israelites for all their sins
t: Once a year, or once for all
p: Hebrews contrasts the yearly repeat with Christ's single offering.
b: The yearly repetition is the point Hebrews takes up: "in these sacrifices sins are called to mind year after year, for the blood of bulls and goats cannot take sins away" (Hebrews 10:3–4). By contrast Christ "has now appeared once, at the end of the ages, to put sin away by the sacrifice of himself" (Hebrews 9:26). Jewish readers answer that Leviticus never claims the blood works by itself: God forgives, the people repent, and the day returns each year because people keep sinning and keep coming back. The closing words, "he did just as the LORD commanded," suggest the first observance happened then (see the variant).
